https://cpj.org/2026/10/journalists-atta.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Amman, October 29, 2026 — The Committee to Protect Journalists condemns the detention of Russian-Israeli journalist Andrey Khrzhanovskiy, known professionally as Andrey X, and U.S. journalist Jasper Nathaniel by Israeli forces near Umm Al-Khair, in the occupied West Bank. The arrests followed a violent assault by Israeli settlers against the two reporters and fellow freelance journalist Adele Shoko. A series of videos and photographs show Israeli settlers attacking Khrzhanovskiy. Shoko reported that settlers beat Khrzhanovskiy, causing him to lose consciousness multiple times, before stealing his phone. The attackers also pepper-sprayed Nathaniel, and took Shoko’s eye glasses. Shoko posted that settlers blocked an ambulance from evacuating Khrzhanovskiy. Attorney Alon Sapir told CPJ that Khrzhanovskiy and Nathaniel are still in police custody in Kiryat 4 station in Hebron. As of publication, authorities have not disclosed the specific legal authority or circumstances surrounding their holding, or the duration of their detention. Sapir confirmed that the two journalists were assaulted yesterday and that Khrzhanovskiy was struck on the head and required medical attention. Shoko claims that they were denied medical treatment for the sustained injuries. Video footage and eyewitness testimonies confirm that Khrzhanovskiy and Nathaniel were detained by Israeli police following their arrival to the scene. “Israeli authorities can’t claim to protect public safety while detaining journalists who have been attacked in the course of their work and failing to hold those responsible for the violence accountable,” said CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah. “Keeping journalists in custody without clearly disclosing the legal grounds for their detention, while they may still need medical care, compounds the harm and sends a dangerous message that those documenting settler violence can themselves become targets of the authorities.” Khrzhanovskiy was briefly detained last week and released after an investigation while filming in Benyamin, in the occupied West Bank. He said that he is facing unsubstantiated charges of “supporting a terrorist organization.” These attacks follow a string of similar incidents affecting local and foreign journalists in the area, including assaults by the Israel Defense Forces on journalists covering a military raid in Hebron, and the deportation of a Portuguese journalist. In September this year, CPJ documented an increase in intensity of settler attacks against journalists in the West Bank. In 2026 alone, CPJ has reviewed at least 16 incidents involving at least 35 local, and international journalists that involved physical attacks, harassment, obstruction, and intimidation of members of the press, the latest incident involving U.S. photojournalist Heidi Levine. CPJ reached out via email to the spokesperson for the Israeli police seeking clarification on the legal grounds, conditions, and whereabouts of the two journalists. No response has been received as of the time of publication. https://novastan.org/en/kyrgyzstan/china.body: 19 August 2026 Kodirjon Eshonkulov Edited by: Mathieu Lemoine Tags CKU Railway Kyrgyzstan Logistics Middle Corridor Uzbekistan Photo: Podrobno.uz Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan For more than two decades, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway existed mainly on planning maps and in diplomatic communiqués. First discussed in the late 1990s, the project was repeatedly delayed by disagreements over financing, track gauge and route. That changed when construction was formally launched in Kyrgyzstan’s Jalal-Abad region in December 2024 . A year later, a syndicate of Chinese banks signed a loan agreement securing the project’s main external financing. For the first time, the railway is taking physical shape rather than remaining a proposal. But its long-term significance will depend on more than steel, concrete and tunnels. The three governments will also have to manage debt, land disputes and environmental risks, while determining where the railway fits within an increasingly complex network of Eurasian trade corridors. The planned route runs for approximately 523 kilometres . It begins in Kashgar in China’s Xinjiang region, crosses into Kyrgyzstan through the Torugart Pass, continues through Arpa and Makmal to Jalal-Abad, and then reaches Andijan in Uzbekistan, where it connects with the existing Uzbek and wider Central Asian rail network. The Torugart Pass on the Kyrgyzstan-China border, through which the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway is planned to run. Photo: Paul / Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA 2.0. China’s railway network uses the 1,435 mm standard gauge, while the existing networks of Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan use the Soviet-derived 1,520 mm gauge. Under the CKU design, the standard-gauge line will extend from China into Kyrgyzstan as far as Makmal. There, a transshipment hub will transfer cargo to trains running on the broader 1,520 mm gauge for the western section of the route. The Kyrgyz section carries most of the project’s engineering difficulty. Roughly 90 percent of the route through Kyrgyzstan passes through mountainous terrain. It will include 29 tunnels and 50 bridges with a combined length of around 120 kilometres – roughly 40 percent of the 304-kilometre Kyrgyz section. A $4.7 billion bet The total cost of the railway is estimated at around $4.7 billion . Under the financing agreement signed in Bishkek in December 2025, approximately half of that amount – around $2.3 billion – is being provided through a 35-year loan from a consortium of Chinese banks led by the China Development Bank and the Export-Import Bank of China. The loan is to be repaid by the joint venture established to build and operate the railway. The remainder is being provided as equity. The joint venture, registered under Kyrgyz law, is 51 percent Chinese-owned, while Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan each hold 24.5 percent . Kyrgyzstan’s equity contribution amounts to approximately $609 million . Around half is to come from the state budget, while the other half is being financed through a $304.5 million preferential loan from China’s Export-Import Bank. The loan has a 25-year maturity, a five-year grace period and an annual interest rate of 1.5 percent. Authorities hope to open the line by 2030, although the scale of the engineering works and the mountainous terrain leave significant room for delays. Kyrgyzstan: transit opportunity, financial exposure For Kyrgyzstan, the railway offers something the country has long lacked: a direct rail connection with China and the possibility of turning its geography from a constraint into an economic asset. President Sadyr Japarov has said that the completed railway will transform Kyrgyzstan “into a transit power” . The government expects transit revenues, new jobs and a stronger role for the country in regional trade. Around 5,000 people are currently employed on the Kyrgyz section, including some 2,000 Kyrgyz citizens. Supporting infrastructure, including substations and transmission lines, is also being built. But the opportunity comes with financial exposure. Kyrgyzstan already owed China’s Export-Import Bank around $1.5 billion in early 2026, making China the country’s largest single external creditor. The new railway adds further liabilities, even if the borrowing terms are relatively favourable. This has prompted debate over whether the project could deepen Kyrgyzstan’s dependence on Chinese financing. The more useful question, however, is not whether the railway fits the contested label of a Chinese “debt trap”, but whether the revenues it generates will ultimately justify Kyrgyzstan’s additional exposure. The loans have long maturities, low interest rates and grace periods intended to keep repayments manageable. Yet future debt servicing will depend in part on transit and logistics revenues that remain projections rather than receipts. There is also a separate question over how much of the economic value generated by the railway will remain inside Kyrgyzstan. If warehousing, customs services, freight consolidation and other higher-value logistics activities are concentrated elsewhere, Kyrgyzstan could gain transit revenue while capturing a smaller share of the wider commercial benefits. Photo: Podrobno.uz. Uzbekistan: the logistics-hub strategy Uzbekistan enters the project from a different position. Andijan is already connected to the country’s national rail network, meaning Uzbekistan does not face the immense engineering challenge of building a new railway across the Tien Shan. Instead, the CKU line would extend Uzbekistan’s transport network eastward and give the country a more direct rail connection with China. That fits a broader Uzbek strategy of turning the country into a logistics hub connecting East Asia, Central Asia and routes leading west and south. Domestic infrastructure has already strengthened this position. The Pop-Angren railway links the Fergana Valley directly with the rest of Uzbekistan without requiring trains to cross neighbouring territory. Tashkent is simultaneously promoting other international routes, including the proposed Trans-Afghan corridor towards Pakistan and transport links across the Caspian towards the South Caucasus, Türkiye and Europe. For Uzbekistan, the CKU railway is therefore not a stand-alone project. Its value lies in how it can connect with a wider network of existing and proposed corridors. If those connections prove commercially viable, Uzbekistan could strengthen its position as one of the principal junctions between China and markets to the west and south. Land, compensation and environmental costs The railway’s benefits are national and regional, but many of its immediate costs are local. Under the intergovernmental arrangements, Kyrgyzstan is responsible for a range of obligations on its territory, including social and environmental impact assessments, protection of cultural heritage, land acquisition, demolition and resettlement. According to the Kyrgyz government, 214 homes are to be demolished to make way for the railway – 191 of them in Suzak district in Jalal-Abad region and the remainder in Naryn. The government says that most affected owners have accepted compensation and that only a small number continue to dispute the amounts offered. However, some residents have publicly challenged the compensation process , while the use of compulsory acquisition has generated public resistance in affected communities . Authorities have hired an independent company to assess the value of affected properties , but questions about transparency, participation and compensation remain sensitive as construction advances. Environmental concerns are also becoming more visible. Kyrgyz regulators have already fined contractors for environmental violations . Special

https://www.azernews.az/oil_and_gas/2664.body: Azerbaijan begins fuel exports to Kyrgyzstan as Bishkek diversifies supplies beyond Russia 30 October 2026 12:27 (UTC+04:00) Akbar Novruz Read more Kyrgyzstan has begun receiving petroleum products from Azerbaijan and several other countries as part of efforts to diversify fuel imports and reduce its dependence on Russia, its traditionally dominant supplier. Kanatbek Eshatov, President of the Association of Petroleum Product Traders of Kyrgyzstan, announced that initial fuel shipments had started arriving from Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Belarus, Türkiye, and China. According to Eshatov, Kyrgyzstan is expanding its network of petroleum product suppliers to reduce the risks associated with relying heavily on a single source. Russia has historically been the country's primary supplier of petroleum products. However, Bishkek is now seeking to broaden its import options to strengthen the stability of domestic fuel supplies. As part of this diversification, the first shipments of fuel from China have also begun arriving in Kyrgyzstan by rail. Eshatov noted that the domestic diesel market remains stable, although some shortages persist in gasoline supplies. Kyrgyzstan's annual demand for petroleum products exceeds 1.5 million tonnes, making reliable imports an important factor in meeting domestic consumption needs. The arrival of Azerbaijani petroleum products marks an expansion of the country's fuel export destinations in Central Asia, while providing Kyrgyzstan with an additional source of supply. The development also reflects Bishkek's efforts to establish a more diversified fuel procurement system involving suppliers from the Caspian region and beyond. However, Eshatov did not disclose the volume or value of the initial Azerbaijani shipments, nor did he specify whether additional deliveries had been agreed. https://www.trend.az/casia/kazakhstan/42.body: Home Central Asia Kazakhstan Air Astana, China Southern ink strategic partnership to expand connectivity Kazakhstan News 30 October 2026 12:28 (UTC +04:00) Photo: Air Astana Alyona Pavlenko Journalist, International Desk Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 30. Kazakhstan's Air Astana and China Southern Airlines signed a strategic partnership agreement on October 30 to strengthen air connectivity between the two countries, expand travel options and improve convenience for passengers, Air Astana's press service announced. The agreement marks the first strategic partnership between airlines from Kazakhstan and China. It builds on their existing codeshare cooperation and provides a basis for further strengthening commercial ties. Under the agreement, the airlines will coordinate flight schedules, expand codeshare services and implement joint marketing initiatives. By bringing their networks and commercial models closer together, the partnership aims to simplify travel on both carriers, provide more convenient connections, align passenger service conditions and rules, and expand access to destinations in Kazakhstan, China and beyond. "More than one million passengers have been carried since the beginning of 2026. The Ministry plans to further expand the route network with China, increasing the number of destinations to 30," Kazakhstan's Deputy Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev said. Air Astana Vice President for Partnerships and Alliances Richard Ledger said that China was a strategically important market for the airline, while Kazakhstan's geographical position made it a transport hub connecting Europe and Asia. He noted that the partnership with China Southern Airlines would help strengthen commercial ties, combine the airlines' complementary route networks and provide passengers with more travel options, convenient connections and more consistent service conditions across both carriers. "China and Kazakhstan are important partners under the Belt and Road Initiative. This strategic cooperation is a significant result of the development of air connectivity between the two countries and reflects our shared commitment to building a prosperous regional market. For both airlines, this is a strategic choice that allows us to leverage each other's strengths and jointly utilize our resources. For passengers, the most tangible benefit will be greater travel convenience, more flight options, simpler transfer procedures and a more comfortable journey," said Zeng Yongchao, Executive Vice President of China Southern Airlines. Air Astana operates flights from Astana and Almaty to Urumqi, Beijing, Guangzhou and Shanghai, offering up to 36 scheduled round-trip flights per week during the peak season. China Southern Airlines operates flights from Urumqi, Beijing, Guangzhou and Xi'an to Almaty and Astana, offering up to 29 scheduled round-trip flights per week during the peak season. The strategic partnership is expected to support business, tourism, educational and family travel between Kazakhstan and China, as well as strengthen transit opportunities for passengers travelling through the two countries to other destinations across the airlines' networks. https://tass.com/politics/2210275.body: Ukraine crisis Foreign journalists to be ‘on ground’ in Alyoshki as tons of aid planned for delivery Preparations for a humanitarian mission in Alyoshki began in May, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said © Alexey Konovalov/TASS MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Dozens of tons of humanitarian aid, including food, sanitary supplies, medicine and fuel, will be delivered to civilians in the town of Alyoshki, Kherson Region, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said. US First Lady Melania Trump has confirmed that American journalists will observe the humanitarian mission. TASS has compiled the key details of preparations for the mission. Preparations for humanitarian mission - Preparations for a humanitarian mission in Alyoshki began in May, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said. - Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov noted that US First Lady Melania Trump had drawn on her extensive experience of humanitarian initiatives to help broker a ceasefire in Alyoshki as part of US peace efforts. Ensuring humanitarian mission security - Russian service members from Battlegroup Dnepr are clearing roads to provide safe passage to Alyoshki, the Russian Defense Ministry said. - Troops are removing unexploded ordnance from the roads leading to the town to facilitate aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians, the ministry added. - US First Lady Melania Trump said late on October 28 that work had begun to ensure the security of the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki. - In addition to clearing mines and other explosive ordnance from roads along the planned route of the humanitarian aid convoy, Russian service members are also helping civilians reach Alyoshki safely. Foreign journalists - Journalists from US television channel Newsmax will "witness and report firsthand" on the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki, Kirill Dmitriev, Russian special presidential envoy for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries and director general of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), said. - US First Lady Melania Trump said later that four Newsmax journalists "will be on the ground" in Alyoshki, "embedded with Russian and Ukrainian humanitarian leaders." - "Serving as neutral observers, they will independently record and permanently document this historic humanitarian mission," Melania Trump added. - TASS published footage from one of its correspondents showing a plane carrying members of the humanitarian mission departing from Moscow. - There were Russian and US journalists on board, including four Newsmax reporters and correspondents from other countries. - Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he considered coverage of the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki by Russian journalists more important than coverage by foreign reporters. Humanitarian aid - The humanitarian operation currently underway in Alyoshki is aimed at providing assistance to civilians, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the Russia-Africa Summit. - Lantratova said that a large humanitarian aid convoy would be assembled to deliver food, medicine and essential supplies to those in need in Alyoshki. - According to her, several dozen metric tons of humanitarian supplies will be delivered to residents of the town. - The human rights commissioner added that the list of supplies had been compiled based on requests from local residents. - The shipment primarily includes food, medicine, sanitary items, fuel and heating supplies. - The Russian Red Cross Society (RRCS) provided humanitarian aid for the residents of Alyoshki, RRCS Chairman Pavel Savchuk said on Telegram. - The Federation of Independent Trade Unions of Russia (FNPR) sent its first truck carrying humanitarian aid to Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, a spokesperson told TASS. - The truck, carrying about 100 boxes containing food, sanitary items and other basic necessities, departed from the FNPR headquarters in Moscow on Thursday. - The aid will be delivered to Alyoshki in the coming days through the FNPR office in the Southern Federal District and the Kherson Region’s trade union organization. Meeting of Russian, Ukrainian representatives - Representatives of Russia and Ukraine involved in the humanitarian operation in Alyoshki departed from Gomel Airport in Belarus aboard the same plane, the BelTA news agency reported. - According to the media outlet, Russian and Ukrainian representatives first saw each other face-to-face at Gomel Airport. - The meeting also involved Belarus, which joined the humanitarian operation. - Belarus is actively participating in this major international activity and has already begun fulfilling its obligations under previously reached agreements, the news agency said. - Minsk is providing Moscow and Kiev with the necessary comprehensive assistance while acting as guarantor of the relevant processes. - Earlier on Thursday, the news agency reported that a Ukrainian delegation led by Human Rights Commissioner Dmitry Lubinets had arrived at the Novaya Guta border crossing in Belarus. https://tass.com/politics/2210737.body: Ukraine crisis Human rights ombudswoman comments on convoy heading to Alyoshki, security arrangements According to Yana Lantratova, the ceasefire, announced in connection with a humanitarian mission in the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, is being respected Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova © TASS MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. The humanitarian convoy organized for residents of the town of Alyoshki in Kherson Region comprises 25 buses, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova told reporters. She also said that a sapper and another person were killed while conducting mine clearance along the routes to ensure the safe passage of the humanitarian mission. TASS has summarized the key statements made by Russia’s Human Rights Commissioner. Ceasefire compliance The ceasefire, announced in connection with a humanitarian mission in the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, is being respected: "The ceasefire in the humanitarian mission zone in Alyoshki is holding. There have been no incidents reported. The Russian and Ukrainian sides are fully meeting their commitments." Mine clearance operations in Alyoshki Two people, including a sapper, were killed while conducting mine clearance operations along the routes to guarantee the safe passage of the humanitarian mission: "A sapper was killed during mine clearance, and another person also died. We extend our condolences to the families and relatives of those who lost their lives." Russian military personnel have finished clearing mines along the routes designated for the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki: "Mine clearance along the routes for the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki has been completed. We thank our military personnel, who put their lives at risk to prepare the roads for safe passage." Residents prepared to evacuate The convoy carrying aid will proceed to the central district hospital: "The convoy will head to the central district hospital." Residents who have decided to leave Alyoshki will be able to do so until 2:00 p.m. Moscow time, with security measures being implemented: "Residents who have decided to leave the town will be allowed to do so until 2:00 p.m. All necessary security measures will be implemented. We plan to begin handing out humanitarian aid after 2:30 p.m." The humanitarian convoy comprises 25 buses: "A large convoy of 25 buses has been assembled for today. They can carry at least 750 people." Special buses for bedridden residents and ambulances are on standby to evacuate people from Alyoshki: "Special buses for bedridden people have been prepared in case they are needed. We have set aside around 30 places for them, as well as nine additional ambulances." A separate bus will be provided for people traveling with their pets as part of the humanitarian mission: "People said they wanted to take their pets with them. We discussed and made arrangements for this as well, so a separate bus will be provided <...> for those who want to take their pets with them." Journalists' coverage Journalists covering the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki will be able to meet and talk to residents in person: "Journalists are also working on site and will be able to speak with residents in person." More than 50 journalists from various countries have come to Kherson Region to report on the humanitarian mission: "Ukrainian journalists, American journalists, journalists from various countries - there are a great many of them, more than 50, so everything is happening openly. This is very important.". https://vlast.kz/novosti/71427-pravitels.body: фото Данияра Мусирова Твитнуть Поделиться Поделиться Поделиться Поделиться Поделиться Тамара Вааль, Астана, Власть Заместитель премьер-министра – министр национальной экономики Серик Жумангарин, рассмотрев депутатский запрос партии «Ак жол» по вопросу установления единой ставки 2-3 % по специальному налоговому режиму на основе упрощенной декларации заявил, что он требует дополнительной оценки. Как напомнил вице-премьер, по новому Налоговому кодексу базовая ставка по специальному налоговому режиму на основе упрощенной декларации составляет 4%. При этом маслихаты имеют право изменять ее и устанавливать в размере от 2 до 6%. В частности, в 2026 году маслихаты Астаны, Алматы, Актобе, Павлодара, Петропавловска и Уральска установили ставку на уровне 3%, а в Шымкенте, Караганде, Атырау, Кызылорде, Таразе, Талдыкоргане, Туркестане, Усть-Каменогорске, Семее и Конаеве – 2%. «Таким образом, действующий механизм уже позволяет устанавливать ставки ниже базового уровня. Вместе с тем вопрос введения единой ставки 2-3% по всей территории страны требует дополнительной оценки с точки зрения влияния на условия ведения бизнеса, доходы местных бюджетов и эффективность действующей модели», - говорится в ответе. Он добавил, что введение единой ставки на республиканском уровне и исключение полномочий маслихатов ограничит учет региональной специфики. А установление ставки 2-3% потребует расчетов бюджетных последствий и оценки изменения налоговой нагрузки для различных категорий предпринимателей. В Миннацэкономики считают целесообразным продолжить мониторинг применения СНР и провести анализ влияния региональной дифференциации ставок на деятельность субъектов МСБ и только по итогам «может быть рассмотрен вопрос о внесении соответствующих изменений». «Таким образом, на данном этапе предложение об установлении единой ставки СНР на основе упрощенной декларации в размере 2–3% по всей территории Республики Казахстан и исключении полномочий маслихатов по ее корректировке не поддерживается», - написал вице-премьер, подчеркнув, что вопрос по совершенствованию действующего механизма стоит рассматривать «по результатам комплексного анализа его практического применения». При этом Жумангарин указывает, что «риска миграции бизнеса между регионами из-за различий в ставках на текущем этапе нет». По его словам, в целом механизм региональной дифференциации не является новым, так как до 2026 года аналогичный подход применялся в рамках специального налогового режима розничного налога. Например, в 2024 году в Алматы сохранялась базовая ставка 4%, в Астане – 3%, в Карагандинской области – 2%, однако, утверждает вице-премьер, «массового перетока бизнеса из Алматы в регионы с более низкой ставкой не фиксировалось». «С 1 января 2026 года принцип региональной дифференциации сохранен в рамках СНР на основе упрощенной декларации и к настоящему времени применяется девять месяцев. При ставке 3% в Астане и 2% в Карагандинской области признаков массовой перерегистрации бизнеса не наблюдается. Это подтверждается и фактическими показателями: по данным формы 910.00 за первое полугодие 2026 года заявленный доход налогоплательщиков вырос в Астане на 23,2%, в Карагандинской области – на 23%, в Алматы – на 18,3%», - привел он статистику. Власть — это независимое медиа в Казахстане. Поддержите журналистику, которой доверяют. https://kaktus.media/doc/555777_vybory_p.body: kaktus.media Выборы президента. Насколько труден тест по кыргызскому языку. Реальный опыт Политика 2983 30 октября 2026 10:33 Kaktus Все самое интересное в Telegram В январе 2027 года в Кыргызстане пройдут выборы президента. Кандидаты обязательно должны пройти тест в "Кыргызтесте" на знание кыргызского языка на уровне не ниже В2. Для справки : уровень B2 ("пороговый продвинутый") - это четвертый уровень владения языком. Он позволяет свободно общаться, учиться и работать в кыргызскоязычной среде. Те, кто владеют языком на таком уровне, могут свободно и спонтанно поддерживать беседу с носителями языка, умеют аргументировать свою точку зрения и вести дискуссии. Распознают речь на слух даже при наличии акцента или на высокой скорости. Читайте также: Выборы президента. Коротко о самом главном (обновлено 28 октября) Илим Карыпбеков на сдаче "Кыргызтеста". Как оказалось, не все носители языка могут сдать экзамен с первого раза. Например, это не получилось у Омурбека Суваналиева и Сыймыка Жапыкеева , которые планировали выставить свои кандидатуры на предстоящих выборах. Жапыкеев решил пересдать: в итоге он набрал необходимые 63 балла. Как проходит тестирование на знание кыргызского языка? Илим Карыпбеков, экс-гендиректор КТРК, а ныне просто блогер (как сказал он сам), сдал тест и рассказал Kaktus.media , как это было. - Почему вы решили попробовать сдать тест? - Я просто решил узнать, насколько хорошо владею языком. Раньше я такой тест никогда не сдавал. Когда-то давно я проходил только TOEFL . Больше я тесты на знание языков не сдавал. Кыргызский язык, конечно, для меня родной, хотя до 9-го класса учился на русском языке. Но 10-й и 11-й классы я окончил на кыргызском. Приехав в Бишкек, понял, что здесь превалирует русский, но тем не менее кыргызский я не забывал. Всегда старался и стараюсь его продвигать. Интересный момент: многие носители языка думают, что они знают кыргызский хорошо, но это не всегда так, к сожалению. Есть разница в обычном, бытовом, языке и в литературной норме. И для работы на госслужбе, конечно, нужно знать хорошо именно литературный язык: для работы с документооборотом и в других сферах нужно владеть на продвинутом уровне. - Как проходила сама процедура сдачи теста? - Я позвонил и спросил про возможность сдать тест. На тестирование надо записываться заранее. Сам тест занимает около двух часов: по полчаса на каждый раздел. Там есть отсчет времени, что позволяет не забывать о времени. Сам тест сдается полностью онлайн. За сдачу четырех блоков - лексики, орфографии, аудирования и сочинения - заплатил 450 сомов. Это достаточно дешево, учитывая, что такая работа выполняется! Когда начал сдавать, понял, что для меня это достаточно легкий уровень. Я могу сдать не только президентский минимум (то есть B2), но и уровень выше - С1. Совсем скоро обещали внедрить проверку на уровень С2. Илим Карыпбеков на сдаче "Кыргызтеста". - То есть сложностей для вас не было? - Особых нет, но были технические особенности. Например, я допускал технические ошибки из-за отличительного интерфейса. На моем компьютере раскладка букв Ң, Ө и Ү отличается. И получилось, что я нечаянно нажал не на те клавиши, и вопрос пропускался. А это означало, что я не ответил на какой-то вопрос. Так что пару баллов я недобрал из-за этого. Всего я набрал 80, 96, 85 и 90 баллов за каждый из блоков соответственно при минимальных 60. При пересдаче мои баллы были бы выше, потому что теперь я уже знаком с интерфейсом. - Что представляют вопросы в тестировании? - Необходимо выбирать вариант ответа. Вопросы касались склонения слов, спряжения глаголов. Где-то было пропущено подлежащее, сказуемое, и надо было выбрать верный ответ. В разделе "аудирование" был небольшой рассказ, который надо было понять и по нему ответить на вопросы. Затем надо было составить связный рассказ. Нельзя посчитать от 1 до 10 или просто наговорить некие слова. А некоторые так и делают, оказывается! Некоторые даже поют. Два блока - на лексику и орфографию - проверяются автоматически, а вот аудирование и сочинение проверяют специалисты - нанятые эксперты кыргызского языка. Поэтому итоговый результат получаешь не сразу. Мне кажется, что здесь есть вариант для каких-то манипуляций, несмотря на то что задания на проверку отправляются анонимно. То есть эксперты не знают, кто сдавал тест. - Искусственный интеллект при сдаче теста не применяется? - На данный момент нет, но, как рассказали специалисты "Кыргызтеста", до конца года они собираются вводить искусственный интеллект и исключить полностью вот этих независимых экспертов, филологов. Искусственный интеллект будет проверять и сразу выводить результаты теста, и только в случае апелляции, когда ты не согласен с "мнением" искусственного интеллекта, комиссионно филологи будут рассматривать результаты. Я понимаю Жапыкеева, когда он сказал, что сомневается в результатах. Наверное, в таких случаях надо публиковать результаты открыто, чтобы была дискуссия и прозрачность в этом вопросе. Но вообще, чтобы завалить этот тест, надо быть абсолютным двоечником. Требуемый для кандидатов в президенты уровень В2 - это уровень знания выпускников школы должен быть. - Как выбирается тема аудирования и сочинения? - Система выдает ее рандомно. Мне для сочинения досталась тема "Благодарность". Да, действительно, здесь нужно использовать слова, которые могут не применяться в обычной жизни. То есть не находятся в активном словарном запасе. Меня также предупредили, что если я просто напишу несколько слов, то тест не будет считаться пройденным. Там необходим объем минимум 15-18 предложений. Илим Карыпбеков на сдаче "Кыргызтеста". - У кыргызского языка есть диалекты. Учитывается ли это при сдаче теста? - Да, говор и диалект считается ошибкой. Об этом меня тоже предупредили. Всякие присказки в речи будут считаться минусом, она должна быть чистой, без слов-паразитов: жатыр-батыр, уникта миякта, например. Есть слова не паразиты, но их говорят по-разному. Но надо использовать литературную норму. У меня был какой-то вопрос, связанный с автомашиной, автотранспортом. Вот я как раз сказал: "Я очень стараюсь говорить без добавления русских и вообще иностранных слов. А в тексте как раз упомянута автомашина, но я говорю "автоунаа". Мне сказали, что такой вариант, конечно, допускается. На месте работают два специалиста - технический, который покажет, что и как делать, а также филолог, у которого можно что-то уточнить, например, по синонимам. Но не просить ответа на вопросы. При тестировании нужно быть внимательным. Могут быть какие-то особенности в тестировании, которые могут ввести в заблуждение. Илим Карыпбеков на сдаче "Кыргызтеста". - Правильно ли обязательное тестирование на знание языка при поступлении на государственную и муниципальную службу? - Лично я согласен с таким решением, потому что давно пора вводить стандарты в документообороте, чтобы все понимали, чтобы все было унифицировано. Надо распространять именно литературный кыргызский язык. У нас многие политики, даже самого высокого ранга, допускают такие банальные ошибки, используют диалектные слова, а это все потом распространяется. Такие тесты используют и в других странах. Люди же сдают TOEFL, IELTS и так далее. Хочется, чтобы скорее внедрили в работу ИИ. Тем более что апелляция при получении результатов предусматривается. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/10/30/taji.body: Share Mehrofarin Najibi , asia+ Categories Governance Tajikistan Format News Published 30.10.2026 16:54 Translations Eng Тоҷ Рус Tajikistan’s lower house of parliament, Majlisi Namoyandagon, has passed a new law aimed at protecting the independence of the country’s statistical authorities and preventing unlawful interference by government bodies and officials. The legislation also introduces electronic reporting, expands access to administrative data and establishes a unified national system of official statistics. The Majlisi Namoyandagon approved the law “On Official Statistics” on October 21, according to the parliamentary newspaper Sadoi Mardum . The government-sponsored legislation will replace the existing Law “On State Statistics,” adopted in January 2010. The new law consists of six chapters and 29 articles. Government interference in statistics to be prohibited One of the key provisions of the new law is a ban on unlawful interference by government bodies and officials in the professional activities of statistical authorities. Jamshed Nurmahmadzoda, director of the Agency for Statistics under the President of Tajikistan, told lawmakers that the provision is intended to safeguard the independence and impartiality of official statistics. He said statistical indicators must be calculated in accordance with scientific and professional standards, without outside influence. The legislation also establishes principles of objectivity, reliability, transparency, accessibility and confidentiality, while strengthening the protection of personal and corporate data. Why is “state statistics” being renamed “official statistics”? According to Nurmahmadzoda, the change reflects a broader reform of how statistical information is collected, processed and published in Tajikistan. While the previous legislation focused primarily on statistical authorities, the new law establishes a national system of official statistics covering all authorized institutions involved in producing and disseminating statistical data. For the first time, this system will formally include not only the Agency for Statistics but also ministries, government agencies, the National Bank of Tajikistan and other authorized bodies. The Agency for Statistics will remain responsible for coordinating the system, including statistical methodologies, reporting programs and the use of data sources. The changes are intended to eliminate duplication in data collection, reduce unnecessary expenses and ensure that statistical indicators produced by different government institutions are comparable. What will change for businesses? The new legislation is also expected to simplify statistical reporting for businesses and reduce their administrative burden. Nurmahmadzoda explained that statistical authorities will be able to obtain administrative data directly from ministries and government agencies rather than repeatedly requesting the same information from businesses. The law also introduces several changes to the reporting system: Statistical reports will be submitted electronically. Electronic signatures and digital data exchange between government institutions will be introduced. Statistical registers will be established to maintain information on enterprises and other reporting entities. Reporting requirements will be clarified, with greater accountability for submitting accurate data on time. According to the head of the Statistics Agency, these measures will streamline data collection and make statistical reporting more efficient. Bringing Tajikistan’s statistics closer to international standards The new law also strengthens the role of the Interdepartmental Council on Statistics, expanding the participation of ministries, government agencies and experts in coordinating statistical activities. Nurmahmadzoda said the reforms are intended to improve the comparability of Tajikistan’s statistical indicators with those of other countries and strengthen public confidence in official data. However, he emphasized that adopting the legislation is only the first step. Its implementation will require closer cooperation between government institutions, improvements in statistical methodologies, further development of digital infrastructure and additional training for statistical professionals. Why is the 2010 law being replaced? According to Nurmahmadzoda, the existing legislation no longer fully meets modern requirements. He cited the growth of the digital economy, the emergence of new data sources, expanding international cooperation and increasingly demanding international statistical standards as the main reasons for the reform. Lawmaker Husniya Ishoqi said the legislation had also been developed in response to recommendations from the United Nations Statistical Commission, Eurostat and the Statistical Committee of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The new law was drafted under the project “Modernization of the National Statistics System in Tajikistan,” with contributions from Tajik and international experts, including Kazakhstan-based StatCentr. The lower house approved the legislation without questions or debate. The law must still be approved by the upper house of parliament, Majlisi Milli, and signed by the president before it can enter into force following official publication. Join us on social media!

https://www.trend.az/casia/kazakhstan/42.body: Home Central Asia Kazakhstan Kazakhstan harvests 24.3 million tons of grain in 2026 - ministry Kazakhstan News 30 October 2026 10:07 (UTC +04:00) Photo: Government of Kazakhstan Alyona Pavlenko Journalist, International Desk Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 30. Kazakhstan harvested 24.3 million tonnes of grain in 2026, one of the country's highest harvests in the past 15 years, with larger volumes recorded in only two previous record years, according to Kazakhstan's Ministry of Agriculture. According to the ministry, grain quality was another important result of the 2026 harvest. Preliminary data show that around 72% of the soft wheat delivered to grain elevators meets third-class standards. Gluten content exceeded 28% in 48% of the samples tested. In Akmola region, third-class wheat accounted for 90%, while Hi-Pro wheat accounted for 70%, according to the ministry. These quality indicators create additional opportunities to use Kazakh grain for food production, develop processing and strengthen the competitiveness of domestic products in international markets. Kazakhstan has also recorded strong export performance. Over the past two marketing years, the country exported 15.5 million tonnes and 16 million tonnes of grain and flour in grain equivalent, respectively. These were record volumes for the years since Kazakhstan gained independence. According to Kazakhstan Temir Zholy, the country's national railway company, grain exports reached 1.657 million tonnes from September through October 19, 2026, up 9%. The volume of mineral fertilizers applied has nearly tripled over the past three years, reaching 1.8 million tonnes in 2025. In 2026, 2.1 million tonnes had been applied against a target of 2.3 million tonnes. The share of elite seeds reached 12%, creating conditions for further improvements in crop yields and agricultural product quality. More than 130,000 tractors, 29,000 combine harvesters, 17,000 reapers and around 130,000 other agricultural machines were used during the 2026 harvest campaign. The depreciation rate of Kazakhstan's agricultural machinery fleet declined from 85% in 2023 to 65% in 2025. The country plans to raise the machinery renewal rate to 8% in 2026. A concessional leasing program is also supporting the modernization of the sector. Since the program was launched, farmers have acquired more than 12,700 tractors and 2,340 combine harvesters. Machinery purchased through the program accounts for nearly 10% of Kazakhstan's total fleet of tractors and combine harvesters. https://www.trend.az/business/4240993.ht.body: Home Economy Azerbaijan's agricultural output exceeds $6.5B in nine months - minister Economy News 30 October 2026 10:49 (UTC +04:00) Photo: Trend News Agency Sadig Javadov Economic Journalist Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 30. Agricultural production in Azerbaijan exceeded 11 billion manat ($6.5 billion) in January-September 2026, Azerbaijan’s Minister of Agriculture, Majnun Mammadov, said during an event held at the ministry’s administrative building to mark November 1 – Agriculture Workers' Day on Friday, Trend ’s correspondent reports from the event. The minister noted that the development of agriculture in Azerbaijan is one of the key priorities of state policy. According to him, the agrarian reforms initiated by National Leader Heydar Aliyev laid a solid foundation for the development of this sector; currently, under the leadership of President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, consistent measures are being implemented to modernize the agrarian sector, enhance its competitiveness, and strengthen food security. Mammadov pointed out that the state program for the development of the production and processing of agricultural, fisheries, and aquaculture products for the years 2026–2030 defines the primary directions for a new phase in the development of the agrarian sector. "Within the framework of this program, key objectives include increasing productivity, implementing modern irrigation technologies, ensuring the efficient use of land and water resources, and expanding production and processing capacities," he remarked. According to the minister, it is essential to continue coordinated efforts with state institutions, the private sector, farmers, and other partners to achieve the goals set out in the state program. He emphasized that improving the legal framework of the agricultural sector, including the adoption of new laws "On seed production" and "On fisheries," as well as the implementation of new approaches to state support mechanisms, serves to create a more favorable operating environment for farmers. Mammadov mentioned that in the first 9 months of 2026, the production of grain crops rose by 8.2% compared to the same period last year, with wheat yields rising to 36.3 centners. Meanwhile, the production of fruits and berries grew by 5%, reaching 842,600 tons. A positive trend was also observed in the export of agricultural and processed products. He added that, despite these results, factors such as climate change, limited water resources, and shifts in international markets necessitate the adoption of more agile and innovative approaches within the agricultural sector. "Digitalization, the implementation of modern technologies, and the integration of scientific knowledge into production must remain the key priorities for agricultural development," the minister explained. The minister also stressed the particular importance of restoring the agricultural potential of the liberated territories. According to him, the establishment of modern farms in Karabakh and East Zangezur, the development of production infrastructure, and the incorporation of land resources into economic circulation are creating new opportunities for the country. https://adcmemorial.org/en/news/witnesse.body: Facebook Twitter Вконтакте Elie Wiesel , a survivor of Auschwitz and Buchenwald and the author of the well-known autobiographical novel Night, wrote that “only those who experienced Auschwitz know what it was; the rest will never know.” As Wiesel saw it, “the witness knew then, as he knows now,” that his experience could not be conveyed or fully comprehended by those who had not been in a concentration camp and had not endured torture and humiliation. The author of the testimony asks: “Others will not know, but will they be able to understand?” And yet, despite his doubts, Wiesel “simply could not remain silent.” Reflecting on the destruction of European Jewry by the German Nazis, Wiesel concludes that over the years not only the actions but also the aims of the antisemites changed: if at the beginning of their rule the Nazis set themselves the task of “building a society without Jews,” towards the end they wanted “to leave behind a world in which Jews seemed never to have existed at all.” Violence against people — Jewish men, women and children — was accompanied by the destruction of the very memory of this people, their culture, language and religion. For many witnesses, the struggle against the destruction of memory became the purpose of their lives, an act of resistance. Contemporary antifascists often repeat that “to remember means to resist,” holding events in memory of comrades killed by neo-Nazis. “Memory Is Resistance” is the slogan on the website of members of Memorial who study the history of political repression in the USSR and preserve testimonies of the horrors of the Soviet past. Memory matters to everyone: both to those who refuse to let themselves or others forget the crimes of the past and the suffering of the victims, and to those who take pride in that past. It is not simply a matter of knowing something — Wiesel was right about that — achieving understanding is much more difficult. We can see how declared aims and ideological attitudes continue to change in our own time. From “Holocaust denial” — until quite recently, apologists for German nationalism claimed that Jews had not been exterminated and had themselves invented both the camps and the crematoria in order to slander innocent Germans (there were even claims that Jews themselves had organised the mass murder of Jews to spite the Aryans) — to contemporary proposals by Alternative for Germany not to teach about Hitlerism in schools and instead devote more attention to Bismarck. Germany’s far-right politicians are now closer to the cynical attitude: “Here’s your beer, here’s your ham, and what happened yesterday is in the past” (the ever-relevant words of a song by Yuliy Kim). No one is saying that it did not happen: it did. The only question is how to regard it, how to understand it. The militarist and nationalist Bismarck is, for the AfD, something good, something to take pride in, while schoolchildren need not be told about certain costs of twentieth-century history: enough already, so much has been said about it. The lavish funeral held in Belgrade with military honours for Ratko Mladić, convicted by the Hague Tribunal of crimes against humanity, is a striking manifestation of the contemporary conflict over memory: for some, the victims and witnesses of crimes matter; for others, what matters is the glorification of war criminals. Everyone wants to remember — but they remember different things and understand the past differently. Those who are erecting ever more monuments to Stalin in the Russian Federation obviously want to remind people of him, often making no attempt to conceal the fact that Stalinism was terror. They simply like terror and want to put it back on a pedestal. And they are prepared to remember the Gulag as well — not to deny its existence, but to explain it in their own way, interpreting it within the framework of the “inadmissibility of distorting the history of the USSR.” Thus, for example, one can hold an academic conference in a former Soviet camp, highlighting “examples of the extraordinary courage and patriotism of our compatriots, whose military and labour achievements have more than once become a central theme of academic conferences organised for ten years by the Perm-36 Museum-Reserve.” But telling the history of the Stalinist era as it was seen by those who survived despite the terror, those who neither forgot nor forgave, is treated as extremism. This is why Memorial was banned and the Gulag History Museum in Moscow was closed. It is not memory that is forbidden — it is understanding that is forbidden, precisely what Elie Wiesel and many others sought to achieve through their testimonies. The struggle to foster an understanding that terror and war crimes are unacceptable does not end even when a verdict has been handed down by the Hague (or Nuremberg) Tribunal. Constant efforts are required not only to prevent people from forgetting, but also to show history — including the most recent history — through the eyes of victims of violence, those who suffered, and surviving witnesses. To show their truth rather than the perpetrator’s version: the perpetrator who does not even conceal what he is doing — who may even take pride in it — but who always has an explanation of his own, most often that he was forced to “strike first,” to assert his right to dominance, and so on. The perpetrators themselves are also eager to preserve the memory of violence — in military monuments, bas-reliefs and installations. The voices of those who suffered can be heard in their memories, accounts and testimonies, which must be collected and published, as is being done today by the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group’s “Voices of War” project and in human rights reports , which bring together the tragic experiences of Ukrainian women and men who have suffered as a result of Russia’s military aggression. Stephania KULAEVA First published on the Radio Svoboda blog Facebook Twitter Вконтакте

HRF calls on India to protect and respect the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. Das and Ranka were arrested and detained during a police crackdown on protests over alleged political bias in the electoral system. The two were taken into custody after reportedly climbing over police barricades to enter a site in central Delhi that had been sealed off by officials. They were subsequently charged with trespassing and disturbing the peace. The Cockroach movement, largely driven by Gen Z students, began amid frustration over school exam leaks and unemployment before expanding into broader concerns over political and governance issues. HRF’s Tyranny Tracker has classified India as ruled by a hybrid authoritarian regime, and space for dissent and civic freedoms continues to shrink. HRF will continue to monitor developments and the state of civic space in India. View post

https://cpj.org/2026/10/iran-sentences-j.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email New York, October 28, 2026—The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Iranian authorities to overturn the convictions and immediately release journalists Artin Ghazanfari and Omid Faraghat . The two were sentenced to 26 and 10 years under Iran’s sweeping espionage law , which also criminalizes routine media activities. “Iranian authorities are using espionage and national security laws to punish journalists for their work, handing down prison sentences that could take decades of their lives,” said Sara Qudah, CPJ’s regional director. “These sentences send a chilling message to every journalist in Iran. Authorities must overturn both convictions, immediately release Artin Ghazanfari and Omid Faraghat, and ensure Ghazanfari receives the medical care he urgently needs.” Ghazanfari, a Bahá’í photojournalist held at Greater Tehran Prison, was sentenced by Branch 15 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Abolqasem Salavati, according to the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) , run by the U.S.-based organization Human Rights Activists in Iran. The verdict was communicated to him on October 26. HRANA reported on October 28 , citing a source close to Ghazanfari’s family, that he received 20 years for “media activities,” five years for “assembly and collusion,” and one year for “propaganda against the state.” The source noted that the judge used Iran’s law on severe espionage punishments to hand down the 20-year term, bypassing the first charge’s standard 10-year maximum sentence. If the verdict is upheld, the longest individual sentence of 20 years could be enforced. Ghazanfari was arrested at his home in Tehran on January 19, 2026. Security agents searched his home and workplace, and confiscated electronic devices, books, and professional equipment. HRANA reported that Ghazanfari suffers from heart failure, high blood pressure , and asthma. Despite prison doctors recommending specialized treatment outside the facility, the judge has reportedly refused to authorize his transfer to a hospital. In a separate case, Branch 2 of the Karaj Revolutionary Court sentenced journalist Omid Faraghat to 10 years and one day in prison and permanently barred him from government and public-sector employment for “media and propaganda activities by producing content and publishing false news online contrary to national security,” according to his cousin, Mohammed Faraghat, who confirmed the details to CPJ, and Mashgh-e Solh , an Iranian news website. IranWire , an independent news outlet covering Iran, reported on October 28, citing the Khabaraneh Telegram news channel run by journalist and former political prisoner Mehdi Mahmoudian , that Faraghat was sentenced under Article 4 of Iran’s 2025 law intensifying punishments for espionage and cooperation with Israel and hostile states . The law also criminalizes certain political, cultural, and media activities, including publishing information authorities deem contrary to national security. Mohammed Faraghat told CPJ that the sentence had not yet been enforced and that the family had challenged the ruling. He said the appeal deadline had been reduced from 20 days to 10 days under the legislation. Faraghat was arrested on June 29, 2026, after being summoned by security police in Karaj, west of Tehran, and has since been held at Karaj Central Prison. He was initially accused of “disturbing public opinion” and “acting against national security.” CPJ emailed Iran’s mission to the United Nations in New York requesting comment but did not receive a response before publication. https://cpj.org/2026/10/cpj-calls-for-re.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email The Committee to Protect Journalists has joined the October 30 Coalition of human rights organizations in issuing a joint statement marking the International Day of Political Prisoners on October 30. The statement underscores the need for sustained international attention to individual political prisoners, for efforts to secure their release, and for accountability for abuses. More than 300 journalists were imprisoned worldwide as of December 1, 2025, according to CPJ’s latest annual prison census , the fifth consecutive year the count has topped that mark. These persistently high numbers reflect rising authoritarianism and a growing number of armed conflicts worldwide. China has been the world’s worst jailer of journalists for three consecutive years, holding at least 50 in 2025. Myanmar, with 30 held, rose from third place in 2024 to second; Israel, with 29 imprisoned, fell from second to third. Azerbaijan, which imprisoned 24, entered the top 10 for the first time since 2018, nearly doubling its prisoner count from the prior year. The numbers imprisoned in Russia, Belarus, Egypt, and Eritrea were consistent with those of the past five years. Israel, the only country on the worst-jailers list that is traditionally considered a democracy, began rapidly imprisoning Palestinian journalists following the start of the Israel-Gaza war in October 2023. Many are imprisoned on undisclosed charges or held without charge in arbitrary detention, in contravention of international law. While Israeli citizens enjoy a broad array of civil rights and freedoms, legal experts identify a radically different standard of justice for Palestinians in the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Israel has arrested more than 110 Palestinian journalists over the course of the war. Journalists are often held in cruel and life-threatening conditions that one freed Palestinian prisoner likened to “a cemetery of the living.” Many imprisoned journalists endure these dangers for years. More than one-third of the journalists counted in the 2025 census are serving sentences of more than five years. Nearly half have never been sentenced at all, and 26% of that group have languished in jail without a sentence for five years or more. Such detentions violate international law , which requires fair trials without undue delay. To reverse the tide of imprisonments, CPJ has consistently called on governments to uphold the rule of law, stop criminalizing journalists who report factually, and hold power to account. CPJ mobilizes political pressure and international expert interventions , leads solidarity campaigns , and takes legal action . With partners, CPJ works to halt or reform legislation that hinders reporting and puts journalists in legal jeopardy. CPJ also provides direct legal, medical, trauma, and other health-related assistance to a growing number of imprisoned and newly released journalists. Over the past five years, the number of journalists receiving both prison and post-prison support from CPJ has risen by nearly 200%. CPJ reiterates its call on governments to release all imprisoned journalists and to rescind policies or laws that criminalize journalism. The international community must uphold the fundamental right to a free press and take the necessary steps to ensure the safety of journalists, particularly those reporting in conflict zones. Read the joint statement here . https://cpj.org/2026/10/somaliland-detai.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email New York, October 28, 2026—The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on authorities in the breakaway republic of Somaliland to release journalist Abdirahman Mohamed Ege, who has been held without charge since October 22 in the city of Hargeisa after interviewing a presidential aspirant. “Abdirahman Mohamed Ege has committed no crime, and the fact that he has been arrested for doing his job is a worrying sign that Somaliland authorities do not respect press freedom,” said CPJ Africa Program Coordinator Muthoki Mumo. “Abdirahman should be released unconditionally and without delay.” On the morning of October 22, Abdirahman was summoned to the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) headquarters in Somaliland’s capital, Hargeisa, and detained upon arrival, according to the Somaliland Journalists Association , and Abdikarim Saed Salah, deputy chairperson of Horn Cable TV, where the journalist works, who spoke to CPJ. Abdikarim, who has visited Abdirahman several times in detention, told CPJ that the journalist was being questioned about his October 15 interview with Abdiqadir Sharay, who plans to stand for the presidency of the Federal Government of Somalia in national elections in 2027. Somalia has a tense relationship with Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991. Somaliland has not been recognized internationally, except for by Israel in December 2025. Abdiqadir was arrested on October 16 in connection with the interview, according to news reports . Somaliland authorities have cracked down on press freedom over the last year, with numerous arrests of journalists and media workers. Journalist Abdiqani Hussein Abokor is also in detention, having been arrested on August 29 after interviewing a poet. CPJ’s October 26 emails requesting comment from Somaliland’s ministry of information and the office of the president did not receive any responses. https://cpj.org/2026/10/how-journalists-.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email The 2026 U.S. midterm elections will take place next week amid a constant drumbeat of press freedom violations , ceaseless vitriol against journalists from the Trump administration, and direct threats to the press across the U.S. Globally, elections are risky for journalists, whether reporting from polling sites or working online. Intensifying attacks against journalists in the U.S. mean newsrooms should already be preparing their staff and freelancers not only for Election Day, but what comes next, and in the weeks and months ahead. “Given the dangerous and evolving landscape for press freedom and journalist safety across the U.S., the importance of safety training and resources for journalists in this country has never been greater. We are paying close attention to local journalists, who face greater risk reporting within their communities during a highly polarized time,” says CPJ Chief Emergencies Officer Lucy Westcott. “Whether it’s digital safety best practices, navigating protest coverage, or making sure journalists know where to get mental health support, we’re helping reporters stay safe amid the crushing reality of being a journalist in the U.S. right now.” Five ways journalists can protect themselves while covering midterm elections Click here Australian reporter Lauren Tomasi, of 9News, was hit by a rubber bullet on Sunday while covering protests against mass deportations in Los Angeles. (Screenshot: 9News-ITV News/YouTube) Intensifying attacks against journalists Journalists across the country, regardless of their medium and beat, are operating amid a roiling emergency and daily threats to their profession and safety. Whether holding a camera, a pen, a phone, or a notebook, more than a decade on from the introduction of “fake news” and “enemies of the people” into the national lexicon, there has been a near-total evaporation of the expectation of press safety in the United States. Moments appear like flashes in the spiral of decline: CNN journalist Omar Jimenez and his colleagues being arrested while on-air in Minnesota in 2020, or Australian journalist Lauren Tomasi leaping in pain after being shot by police while reporting live from protests in Los Angeles in 2025. CNN correspondent Omar Jimenez and his colleagues were arrested while on-air while covering protests in Minnesota in 2020. (Screenshot: CNN/YouTube) Those covering the U.S. midterms are reporting within a drastically decaying environment for press freedom and safety. Since the beginning of 2026, 166 press freedom violations have been recorded against journalists by the U.S. Press Freedom Tracker, including arrests, assaults, and the issuing of subpoenas, all connected to their reporting. CPJ has seen a marked increase in requests for physical, digital, and psychosocial safety assistance from U.S.-based journalists, who know this training and knowledge is now crucial to keeping them safe while reporting. In 2021, CPJ supported 34 U.S.-based journalists with safety training and emergency financial support, which swelled to 959 journalists just four years later, a more than 2,000 percent increase. The U.S. Journalist Assistance Network (JAN) was created in 2025 to give an ever-growing number of U.S.-based journalists a fast and direct way to access support, training, and safety information. How CPJ has supported journalist safety in 2026 Declining press freedom in the U.S. and heightened risks for journalists has impacted not only the physical and digital safety of reporters, but also their mental health. Amid intense immigration crackdowns in Minnesota earlier this year, CPJ quickly set up with partners an emergency fund to support more than two dozen local journalists on the frontlines of this coverage with mental health support and personal safety equipment. CPJ has spoken with newsrooms serving diaspora populations who report feeling exhausted and anxious about continued immigration enforcement in their communities. In Minnesota, journalists told CPJ of the disbelief that the violence they witnessed could happen in the cities they call home. Editors covering Minnesota endured 24-hour shifts, reviewing graphic images and testimony, and carrying the colossal weight of caring for their journalists on assignment. CPJ and our partners have long supported journalists in the U.S. with mental health support, and will continue as long as journalists need it. Across the country, CPJ has so far in 2026 provided more than 400 journalists with physical, digital, psychosocial, and legal safety training, including safety workshops focused on this election. Digital safety and intensifying surveillance across internet platforms are primary safety concerns for journalists in the U.S., with nearly 60 percent of CPJ’s 2025 safety training workshops including digital safety as a primary focus. A CNN sticker is seen on equipment in the James Brady press briefing room of the White House on September 19, 2026 in Washington, DC. The White House made good on US President Donald Trump’s vow to deny CNN, MS NOW and Politico access to the presidential mansion as punishment for reporting what he calls “fake news.” The three news outlets denounced the ban as a violation of the US constitution and vowed to keep reporting on the US government. (Photo: AFP/Oliver Contreras) How to shore up press freedom in the U.S. As CPJ continues to keep journalists across the U.S. safe, attacks against the press have taken on an even sharper edge as the midterms have drawn closer. Following the ban on news outlets CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from accessing the White House, CPJ joined a legal effort to restore their access. While it remains in place for now, the ban marks “one of the most aggressive uses of legal powers against the press in the United States in decades,” says Jose Zamora, CPJ’s Americas Regional Director. Similarly, government directives under the Trump administration have been weaponized to crackdown on press freedom, undermine the rule of law, and block Congress from upholding its oversight role in protecting First Amendment rights. Journalists and media outlets have been threatened with retaliation over unfavorable news coverage as part of an intensifying system of repression that lawmakers must move quickly after midterms to dismantle. Intensifying attacks against journalists in the U.S. mean newsrooms should already be preparing their staff and freelancers not only for Election Day, but what comes next, and in the weeks and months ahead. (Photo: Reuters/Nathan Howard) “Tactics to suppress the press that are the hallmarks of authoritarian regimes have become the norm under the current US administration,” said CPJ CEO Jodie Ginsberg. “A free press is a fundamental public good. Those elected to serve the American people need to rediscover a backbone and rigorously defend a free press. Media organizations must equally refuse to be bullied and stand forthright in their defense of the First Amendment.” The litany of government-led attacks against the press has sparked national attention over the past year. At least 10 journalists have been subpoenaed this year in publicly reported cases as the Trump administration has attempted to stem government leaks by using subpoenas to pressure journalists to reveal their sources. Journalists reporting on protests face unprecedented charges, including independent reporters Don Lemon and Georgia Fort, who were arrested along with other journalists while covering a protest in a St. Paul church. They face felony charges, including under the KKK Act that is intended to protect Black Americans’ constitutional rights. Press access continues to be squeezed and shuttered. New and stringen

https://cpj.org/2026/10/cpj-partners-con.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email The Committee to Protect Journalists and 129 organizations condemn the conviction of Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr, and denounce the court’s order to shut down one of the country’s last remaining independent newsrooms. In a joint statement, rights organizations urged Egyptian authorities to allow Mada Masr to operate freely, and stop weaponizing media permit laws to arrest and prosecute journalists. “The order to shut down Mada Masr, one of Egypt’s leading media outlets, is outrageous and a clear signal that Egypt is doubling down on its efforts to suppress independent media,” said CPJ CEO Jodie Ginsberg. “The world cannot keep watching in silence as Egypt’s independent journalism dies, while Egyptian journalists risk their freedom to keep the public informed.” On October 27, the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court convicted Attalah of managing an unlicensed website and imposed the maximum penalty, a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (about US$54,000) and the closure of Mada Masr’s website. Attalah was taken into custody inside the courthouse immediately after the ruling, and released approximately seven hours later. The ruling is part of an unprecedented crackdown on the press in Egypt, which recently saw the arrest of the entire newsroom of the investigative platform Matsadaash, and the summoning of journalist Rasha Azab . Egypt remains one of the world’s worst jailers of journalists, with at least 25 currently behind bars . Read the full statement in English and Arabic .
