https://cabar.asia/en/violation-of-right.body: © CABAR - Central Asian Bureau for Analytical Reporting Please make active links to the source, when using materials from this website From February 2025, the new law “On the freedom of religion and religious associations” signed by President Sadyr Japarov at the end of January becomes effective in Kyrgyzstan. According to experts, the law contains restrictive measures, yet they believe that new regulations will help the state solve a number of issues. What is the law for? The president’s press service announced the signing of the law on January 21 and noted the new document is going to ensure the freedom of religion and determines the status, rights and obligations of religious actors. According to the presidential administration, the law contains a clearer procedure of interaction between the state and religious organisations, activity of religious educational institutions, sets forth a list of prohibited actions in religious activity, as well as regulates other matters related to religion. Azamat Yusupov, head of the State Committee for Religious Affairs, speaking before the parliament in December, said in detail which issues are faced in the religious sphere and why the new law is needed. He said that the current law “On the freedom of religion and religious associations” – the main document regulating the religious sphere – was outdated. “Many issues that now prevent from pursuing the effective religious policy are not specified in the current law. For example, the order of importation of religious literature to Kyrgyzstan, chaotic construction of religious projects, arrangement of the process in religious education, departure of citizens abroad for religious education, uncontrolled distribution of religious literature on the streets and in public places, door-to-door visits of various religious groups and forcing values of various religious movements, arrangement of activities of various foreign religious missionaries and charitable foundations,” Yusupov said. According to him, the new law is required to solve all the issues voiced by him and to pursue a correct state policy in the sphere of religion. “Since independence, citizens go abroad to obtain religious education, come back with various methods of religious propagation, which lead to the creation of various communities, some of which do not take the muftiate seriously, privatize religious buildings, and divide the society into various groups. There have been facts when citizens reject to get education and turn away from modern medicine,” Yusupov said. He noted that there have been cases when the academic process in religious educational institutions is out of control. Besides, representatives of diverse religious groups began to spread their ideas and adopt their approaches. “As a result, as you know, there was a problem when thousands of citizens began to leave for Syria. Given these problems, the State Committee together with state bodies and a group of experts developed the new draft law, which was discussed with the representatives of all religions,” he said. According to him, the country has been monitored for the last three years, and a whole list of problems to be solved by the state was compiled. Ait namaz (prayer) in the central mosque of Bishkek, 16.06.2024. Photo: Press Service of the President of KR Dawah — a main stumbling block? The process of law adoption took several months. It was first brought up for public discussion by the State Committee for Religious Affairs in August 2024. Right after, the public began to argue over some provisions, for example, a ban on door-to-door visits with the purpose of spreading the religion. Some activists called it back then as the law against dawa – a way to involve citizens into religion through visiting their houses and apartments by representatives of mosques or religious associations. However, Askat Alagozov, press secretary of the President, refuted it, and asked the society not to spread provocative messages, saying it was incorrect to call the law regulating the religious sphere in the country as the initiative ‘against the dawah’. Some lawyers and experts have expressed their opinion saying that the law was ‘unfinished’ and it was needed a modification. In early September, it became known that President Sadyr Japarov held a meeting with religious activists, and it was decided on the basis of it that the document would be modified and only then would be submitted to Zhogorku Kenesh. The modified law was submitted to the parliament last November. It contains such fundamental norms as warranty of the freedom of religion, and a ban on conversion to any religion by psychological and physical violence. According to the document, the state does not interfere with the work of religious organisations, if they comply with the law, do not fund activities of religious organisations, and do not hold political events in places of worship. At the same time, the document contains provisions prohibiting religious associations and religious figures from intervening into politics – they cannot establish parties or take part in elections of the president and members of parliament, fund parties or take part in election campaigning. During the discussion in the parliament, deputy Zhalolidin Nurbaev asked his colleagues to discuss the document thoughtfully. In his opinion, the people who give the dawah help influence the young people in remote areas, who stop committing illegal or improper actions in moral terms once they follow the path of religion. “The dawah is calling the people to the good and an attempt to lead the people away from the wrong path. Now they are offering to ban it. If we recall our situation 25 years ago, many people were unaware of religion and many young people were involved in theft, used alcohol, and committed violence. It was due to the dawah that religion spread. One of the important achievements was that there was no longer regionalism there,” the parliamentarian said. Later on, during the discussion of the law, Azamat Yusupov, the head of the State Committee for Religious Affairs, refuted information about the intention to ban the dawah. He said that there was a misunderstanding in the society and explained that the state was planning to ban the door-to-door visits, while the dawah could be given by other means. “The dawah is not only a door-to-door visit, it can be writing books, group or YouTube training. We simply say that it should be performed in a certain way. All parties to the discussion have reached this opinion – we, experts, representatives of the muftiate. We are not banning the dawah, it is out of the question. The question is only the ways of dawah. There are various sects, both registered and unregistered, which use the door-to-door approach. There are extremist groups, which are banned by law, and they use this approach, too,” Yusupov said. A week after this speech, the State Committee for National Security reported the neutralization of the ‘largest structural network of the religious and extremist organisation ‘Hizb ut-Tahrir’. The security service reported that 22 detained persons in Dzhalal-Abad region were teaching extremist ideology to citizens, and also distributed leaflets against the new version of the law “On the freedom of religion and religious associations” among religious organisations. By results of the draft law discussion, members of parliament did not exclude the provision banning the door-to-door visits. According to him, the document contained only one controversial issue – door-to-door visits for the purpose of preaching. He noted that citizens with secular views were against such door-to-door visits. https://novastan.org/de/politik-und-wirt.body: 27. Oktober 2026 Niklas Birli Schlagwörter Afghanistan Shanghaier Organisation für Zusammenarbeit Sicherheit SOZ Tadschikistan Turkmenistan Usbekistan Die Staatschefs der Mitgliedstaaten der SOZ beim jährlichen Gipfel 2026 in Bischkek, Kirgisistan. Foto: Website des Präsidenten der Republik Aserbaidschan. Beim 25. Gipfel der Shanghaier Organisation für Zusammenarbeit in Bischkek haben sich die Mitgliedsstaaten der Organisation auf die Bischkek-Erklärung geeinigt, welche die Notwendigkeit einer inklusiven und stabilen Herrschaft in Afghanistan betont. Seit dem Russischen Überfall auf die Ukraine im Jahr 2022 haben die zentralasiatischen Länder neues Interesse an ihrem Nachbarn und erhoffen sich wirtschaftliche und sicherheitspolitische Zusammenarbeit. Dies kommt den Taliban, welche seit 2021 autokratisch über Afghanistan herrschen, durch die prekäre Wirtschaftslage im eigenen Land überaus gelegen. Selten hat ein Geburtstag so viele prominente Gäste: Zum 25jährigen Bestehen der Shanghaier Organisation für Zusammenarbeit (SOZ) erschienen zum diesjährigen SOZ-Gipfel in Bischkek neben dem russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin der chinesische Führer Xi Jinping , der indische Premierminister Narendra Modi , aber auch Massud Peseschkian aus dem Iran. Aus Zentralasien waren, neben dem Gastgeber Kirgistan, die Staatsoberhäupter der Gründungsmitglieder der Organisation, Kasachstan, Tadschikistan und Usbekistan anwesend, um sicherheits- und wirtschaftspolitische Fragen zu diskutieren. Lest auch auf Novastan : Warum die Shanghaier Organisation für Zusammenarbeit ihre Relevanz verloren hat Dabei waren sich die geopolitisch oft miteinander konkurrierenden Staaten in einem Punkt erstaunlich einig: Die Rolle des abwesenden Staats Afghanistan für das Sicherheitsgefüge der Region und die Notwendigkeit von Stabilität im Land seit der erneuten Machtübernahme der Taliban im August 2021 , welche nicht eingeladen worden waren. Der stellvertretende SOZ-Generalsekretär Ahmad Saeed Moradzadeh betonte in einer Rede die Notwendigkeit internationaler Unterstützung und die Abfederung ausfallender Handelseinnahmen, um die humanitäre Katastrophe des Landes zu bekämpfen; die gemeinsame Position der Teilnehmerstaaten wurde in der sogenannten Bischkek-Erklärung festgehalten. Von der gewalttätigen Herrschaft der Taliban, welche von dem UN-Sonderberichterstatter für Menschenrechte in Afghanistan, Richard Bennett , als Gender-Apartheid aufgrund der systematischen und institutionalisierten Diskriminierung von Frauen bezeichnet wird, war dagegen keine Rede. Afghanistan, angrenzend an den Iran, Tadschikistan, Turkmenistan, Usbekistan, China sowie Pakistan, ist allein durch seine geografische Stellung ein verbindendes Sicherheitsrisiko. Ein Jahr zuvor hatten sich in Taschkent die zentralasiatischen Staaten erstmals im sogenannten Termez-Dialog getroffen, um ihr gemeinsames Vorgehen hinsichtlich Afghanistans abzustimmen, unter anderem bei den Themen politischer Dialog, Verkehr und Logistik, Klima sowie kulturell-humanitäre Zusammenarbeit. Taschkent versucht, wie eurasianet berichtet , Afghanistan nicht ausschließlich als Sicherheitsrisiko, sondern als Baustein einer möglichen regionalpolitischen Erschließung zu betrachten. Unterstützt Novastan – das europäische Zentralasien-Magazin Als vereinsgetragene, unabhängige Plattform lebt Novastan vom Enthusiasmus seiner ehrenamtlichen Mitarbeiter:innen – und von eurer Unterstützung! Novastan unterstützen Denn die Ansätze der zentralasiatischen Länder, wie mit dem neuen Regime in unmittelbarer Nachbarschaft umzugehen ist, unterscheiden sich noch deutlich voneinander: Usbekistan, welches sich von den zentralasiatischen Staaten am aktivsten für eine regionale Integration Afghanistan einsetzt, ohne aber die Taliban anzuerkennen, hat sich für einen pragmatischen Weg entschieden, indem die begrenzten diplomatischen Kanäle für Sicherheits- und Handelsfragen genutzt werden. Tadschikistan, wahrscheinlich in Anbetracht seiner Erfahrungen im Tadschikischen Bürgerkrieg 1992-1997 , in dem islamistische Akteure, unterstützt durch die Taliban, tadschikische Flüchtlinge für den Kampf gegen Duschanbe rekrutierten , setzt vermehrt auf Sicherheitsmaßnahmen . Dies äußert sich vor allem im Ausbau der Grenzanlagen mit chinesischer Unterstützung an der tadschikisch-afghanischen Grenze. Es kommt primär zum Austausch, um Konflikte zu entschärfen, wie beim Beschuss chinesischer Arbeiter:innen im Grenzgebiet von afghanischer Seite im vergangenen Jahr. Lest auch auf Novastan : Tadschikistan: Schwierige Nachbarschaft mit den Taliban Diese beiden Pole offenbaren die Vielseitigkeit der zentralasiatisch-afghanischen Beziehungen. Afghanistan ist keineswegs erst jetzt auf die außenpolitische Agenda seiner Nachbarn gekommen: Schon in den 1990ern, kurz nach der eigenen Unabhängigkeit, intervenierten Usbekistan und Tadschikistan im damaligen Bürgerkrieg, um afghanische Tadschik:innen und Usbek:innen gegen die Taliban zu unterstützen. Seit dem Russischen Überfall auf die Ukraine 2022 hat das Thema allerdings neue Brisanz erfahren. Die Tendenz neigt zur wirtschaftlichen Integration Afghanistans, wie beispielhaft das Wirtschaftsprojekt TAPI zeigt: Mit TAPI (Turkmenistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan und Indien), dessen afghanischer Bauabschnitt im Oktober 2025 mit einer Eröffnungsfeier im afghanischen Herat in Anwesenheit von Turkmenistans ehemaligen Herrscher Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov zelebriert wurde , wird eine Erdgaspipeline geplant, um aus dem turkmenischen Gasfeld Galkynysch über 1800 Kilometer eine Gasmenge von 33 Milliarden Kubikmeter Erdgas pro Jahr über Afghanistan und Pakistan bis nach Indien zu transportieren. Diese Pläne, welche bereits seit den 1990ern existieren, werden nun verstärkt verfolgt. So traf sich dafür der stellvertretende Vorsitzende des Ministerkabinetts Afghanistans für Wirtschaftsfragen, Abdul Ghani Baradar , mit Berdimuhamedow , nun Vorsitzender des turkmenischen Volksrats, um Mechanismen zwischen den jeweiligen Behörden zum Vorantreiben des Projekts zu schaffen. Die Taliban wollen nach eigenen Angaben von den turkmenischen Erfahrungen in der Gasindustrie profitieren . Dabei bleibt es nicht nur bei einer Pipeline. Vielmehr steht TAPI symbolisch für eine stärkere Integration Afghanistans in der Region in den Bereichen Eisenbahn, Strom, aber auch Wirtschaftskooperation. Afghanistan, der „Inbetweener“ zwischen Süd- und Zentralasien, wird also zu einem Schlüsselgebiet der regionalen Wirtschaftserschließung. Auch hier zeigen Zentralasiens Regime außenpolitische Flexibilität. Nur so lässt sich erklären, weshalb islamistische Gruppen in den zentralasiatischen Ländern bekämpft werden, gleichzeitig aber die Zusammenarbeit mit den Taliban akzeptiert wird. Lest auch auf Novastan : Turkmenistan liefert Gas durch afghanisches Territorium nach Pakistan Dies kommt auch den neuen Herrschern Afghanistans entgegen: Die Taliban werden aller Wahrscheinlichkeit nach verstärkt die Nähe zu den zentralasiatischen Nachbarn suchen, da das Verhältnis zum südasiatischen Nachbarn Pakistan bis zuletzt von außenpolitischen und militärischen Spannungen geprägt ist. Im Februar 2026 kam es zum Zusammenbruch einer fragilen Waffenruhe und einer offenen Kriegserklärung Pakistans an die Taliban, da ihnen vorgeworfen wurde, terroristischen Gruppen Unterschlupf zu gewähren. Seit 2021 sind Wirtschaft und Handel im Land zusammengebrochen, die Taliban müssen sich durch Drogenhandel und Entführungen über Wasser halten . Umso attraktiver erscheinen nun die Wirtschaftsprojekte und Visionen der zentralasiatischen Nachbarn, die Region besser zu erschließen und ein wirtschaftliches Gegengewicht zu Russland zu schaffen. Daher überrascht es nicht, dass es dieses Jahr am fünften April zum ersten afghanisch-zentralasiatischen konsultativen Dialog in Kabul kam, bei dem die Taliban mit den zentralasiatischen Staaten Möglichkeiten der gemeinsamen Zusammenarbeit diskutierten. https://24.kg/en/article/kyrgyzstan-to-l.body: Kyrgyzstan is preparing to launch a unified digital platform to screen, license and monitor participants in the virtual asset market. The system will help identify companies and their owners subject to international sanctions, the National Agency for Virtual Assets and Blockchain Technologies under the President of the Kyrgyz Republic (NAVA) told 24.kg news agency . According to the agency, the new platform will screen not only cryptocurrency companies but also their executives and ultimate beneficial owners. Digital verification mechanisms, sanctions lists and blockchain analytics tools will be used for this purpose. The information collected will be taken into account when reviewing license applications and assessing the risks associated with market participants’ activities. NAVA said the initiative is aimed at reducing sanctions risks, improving state regulation and introducing international standards in the virtual asset sector. Cryptocurrency market regulation was discussed at the third meeting of the National Council for the Development of Virtual Assets and Blockchain Technologies, held in September 2026 under the chairmanship of President Sadyr Japarov. Following the meeting, the authorities were tasked with improving legislation, strengthening oversight and establishing unified risk management mechanisms. The National Council has endorsed the initiative to launch the digital platform. According to the agency, the system is also expected to improve information sharing between government bodies and make oversight of the cryptocurrency market more effective. The launch date, development cost and specific procedures for conducting sanctions checks have not yet been disclosed.

https://kz.kursiv.media/en/2026-10-28/en.body: Kazakhstan and China discuss Shymkent Oil Refinery expansion and oil supplies Published October 28, 2026 12:36 Nikolai Marchenko Senior Journalist n.marchenko@kursiv.media Svetlana Voronova Photo: Primeminister.kz The expansion of the Shymkent Oil Refinery was one of the main topics of talks between Kazakhstan and China’s CNPC in Astana. The joint venture’s annual processing capacity is expected to double to 12 million tons. The project was reviewed at the fifth meeting of the working group on Kazakhstan-China cooperation in the oil and gas sector, chaired by Kazakhstan’s First Deputy Prime Minister Nurlybek Nalibayev . Participants included Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov , CNPC President Zhou Xinhuai and representatives of oil and gas companies from both countries, the government’s press service said . Alongside the refinery expansion, the parties discussed increasing oil supplies and pipeline capacity, expanding geological exploration, and cooperation in the gas sector, petrochemicals and new energy. They also reviewed the extension of existing subsoil use contracts and issues related to joint projects. Shymkent Oil Refinery: What was discussed Akkenzhenov also held a separate meeting with the president of CNPC. According to the Energy Ministry , during Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to China in fall 2025, the parties agreed to consider expanding the Shymkent Oil Refinery as a standalone initiative. At the latest talks, they discussed the project’s status and next steps. The minister noted that CNPC has been one of Kazakhstan’s key strategic partners for more than 30 years. Participants also discussed developing gas and petrochemical projects, fulfilling contractual obligations, increasing the share of Kazakhstani goods and services and training personnel. China’s participation in the project The Shymkent Oil Refinery is a joint venture between KazMunayGas and CNPC. In June 2025, the companies and the Energy Ministry signed a framework agreement to double the refinery’s capacity. The expansion is expected to be completed by 2030. The East China Engineering Design Institute is involved in preparing the feasibility study. The refinery will add a new processing line with a capacity of 6 million tons of oil per year. To ensure a sufficient supply of crude oil to the refinery, KazMunayGas (KMG) and CNPC are also preparing to expand the Kenkiyak-Atyrau oil pipeline to a capacity of 15 million tons per year and the Kenkiyak-Kumkol oil pipeline to 20 million tons per year. The companies agreed to develop the project documentation at a meeting on Oct. 22. Share Link copied

Today, 14:00 2 min read 2 508 views 0 comments 0 Source: Althawranews Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei has explained that posts published by Iranian diplomatic missions about Samarkand were intended as an appeal to the U.S., following objections from Uzbekistan over the portrayal of the historic city’s cultural heritage. “ “Some of our friends in embassies had posted their posts as an appeal to the U.S. side,” Baghaei said, commenting on social media posts that prompted a reaction from Uzbekistan. Baghaei also emphasized the longstanding ties between Iran and Uzbekistan, expressing confidence that their shared cultural heritage would help strengthen relations between the two countries. “ “The ties that bind Iran and Uzbekistan did not arise today or yesterday. We attach great importance to our relations with Uzbekistan,” he said, adding that their common heritage could serve as a basis for continuing friendly relations between the two peoples. On October 23, Uzbekistan’s Foreign Ministry summoned Iranian Ambassador Mohammed Ali Eskandari and handed him a note of protest over posts published by Iranian embassies in Armenia, Zimbabwe, Bulgaria and other countries. The posts presented Samarkand’s historical and cultural heritage in what Tashkent described as a one-sided and political manner. Uzbekistan’s Foreign Ministry stressed that the heritage of Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva forms an integral part of the Uzbek people’s centuries-old history and traditions of statehood. It called on Iranian diplomatic missions to remove the relevant posts and prevent similar incidents in the future. The posts followed U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Samarkand and his video message from Registan Square. Iranian diplomatic missions responded to the video with posts portraying Samarkand’s architecture as part of Persian or Iranian-Islamic civilization. https://cabar.asia/en/could-central-asia.body: © CABAR - Central Asian Bureau for Analytical Reporting Please make active links to the source, when using materials from this website На русском Given the high mobility of these foreign jihadists, they could spread instability across the entire Middle East, Africa, and the global community. Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham supporters in the Syrian city of Hama. Photo: Ghaith Alsayed/AP/dpa/picture alliance Analysts fear that the new Kabul regime will inspire extremist organisations across the region. In early January, Tajik national Saifiddin Tojiboev was reportedly appointed head of operational headquarters in the ministry of defence of the new Syrian government. The 41-year-old, a native of Spitamen district in the Sughd region of Tajikistan, was one of the commanders of the militant wing of Jama’at al-Tawhid wal-Jihad, a group allied with the ruling Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) movement. Most of the group’s fighters are from Central Asian countries. Tojiboev’s reportedly high position is recognition that the contribution of Central Asians to defeating Bashar al-Assad was significant. Following the fall of that regime, questions remain over the future of these foreign fighters, with fears that they could pose a significant future security threat. Considering the high mobility of these foreign jihadists, it can be argued that this threat extends to the entire Middle East, Africa, and the global community. There is little verified data on the number of Central Asian citizens who are currently in various military formations in Syria. Media reports have focused on citizens of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, although there are also fighters from Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan among the insurgents. In November 2018, the State Committee for National Security of Tajikistan reported that about 1,900 Tajik citizens had travelled to Syria and Iraq to fight in Islamist organisations in recent years. Tojiboev was among them. Previously a member of the banned Islamic Renaissance Party of Tajikistan (IRPT), for a time he even headed a party cell in Spitamen district. Dushanbe declared the IRPT a terrorist organisation in 2015 and dozens of its activists, including many leaders, were imprisoned. In Tajikistan, Tojiboev remains on the list of individuals charged with terrorism and the authorities have previously accused him of recruiting Tajik citizens “into the ranks of terrorist groups”. A source in Tajikistan’s security services told local media on January 5 that they were aware of Tojiboyev’s appointment. He said Tojiboev travelled to Syria with his brother in 2013. Most Tajik nationals who travelled to the region joined the ranks of the Islamic State (IS) group. They included Gulmurod Khalimov, a former commander of the Tajik interior ministry’s special purposes mobile unit, who was reportedly even appointed IS so-called minister of war. In August 2016, the US described Khalimov as a “key leader” in IS and announced a three million US dollar reward for information about him. The following month, following the death of IS chief strategist Abu Mohammad al-Adnani, Khalimov was described as the second most important person in IS after its leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi. According to media reports, Khalimov was killed in an airstrike in Mosul in April 2017. Following the defeat of IS, some Central Asia militants relocated to Afghanistan, where they joined the Islamic State of Khorasan (IS-KP), an IS affiliate operating in Afghanistan. In a 2019 UN report presented to the Security Council, another native of Tajikistan, Sayvali Shafiyev, was named as the leader of ISKP. The report stated that the group, which operates in Afghanistan’s Nangarhar province, had more than 200 fighters. According to UN experts, Shafiyev was also recruiting new fighters for the ISKP and fundraising online. Another influential Tajik national, Shamil Hukumatov, was also one of the leaders of the ISKP. In June 2023, he was arrested in Istanbul, where he was raising money and recruiting new fighters for ISKP. Lucas Webber, a researcher at the Soufan Centre, an international intelligence organisation, has stated that IS-Khorasan “expanded its influence in Central Asia following the withdrawal of US forces from Afghanistan”. Central Asians have also been involved in a number of international terror attacks in recent years. In July 2023, Germany and the Netherlands detained six Tajik nationals on suspicion of terrorism and in January 2024 Tajik nationals were also suspected of carrying out attacks in Kerman and Shiraz in Iran. On March 22, 2024, Tajik migrants, apparently acting on the instructions of IS operatives, attacked the Crocus City Hall near Moscow killing more than 100 people. Last summer, eight men from Tajikistan were arrested in the US for alleged ties with IS, while in November 2024, three Uzbek nationals were arrested in the UAE on suspicion of murdering Israeli-Moldovan rabbi Zvi Kogan. Regarding Central Asians in Syria, there are several possible scenarios, each with its own risks. One is that the Damascus authorities, under pressure from the international community and in order to preserve internal stability, will decide to expel foreign fighters. There are already voices in Syria demanding this. Following rumours that it was foreign fighters who set fire to a Christmas tree in a Christian neighbourhood in Damascus, a December 23 protest heard locals chant slogans against the presence of foreign fighters in Syria. “Syria is free, non-Syrians must leave,” protesters said. Most foreign fighters are unlikely to abandon the idea of jihad, and will probably relocate to other conflict zones, as happened following the defeat of IS. For Central Asian militants, the most probable destination is Afghanistan, where ideologically aligned IS factions are already active. However, other destinations such as Mali, cannot be ruled out. There are also widespread concerns in Central Asia that citizens who fought in foreign wars might return and attempt to cause serious unrest, although there have been no public announcements as to policy. In recent years, Central Asian governments have returned hundreds of fighters and their family members from Iraq and Syria, attempting to reintegrate them. The situation is exacerbated by diminishing economic opportunities at home accompanied by worsening conditions for Central Asian migrants in Russia. This group has long been a key recruitment pool for radical Islamist groups; Dushanbe claims most Tajiks who fought abroad were recruited from the ranks of labour migrants. It is also crucial not to overlook the presence of sleeper cells of radical Islamic group supporters in Central Asia, who actively recruit new members and orchestrate terrorist attacks both within the region and in Russia. In Syria, installing foreign fighters such as Tojiboev in senior positions might raise concerns in other countries. The new authorities in Syria had made clear that had no ambitions of pursuing global jihad, but the appointment of foreign citizens connected to various radical organisations in their home countries could signal different intentions. If supporters of a global caliphate gain significant power in Syria, a return to the days when IS sought to spread its ideology worldwide through terrorist acts might be possible. https://24.kg/en/article/57-companies-to.body: In Kyrgyzstan, 52 legal entities have ceased operations as part of efforts to minimize sanctions risks, while compulsory liquidation procedures are underway against another 57 companies. State-owned banks have also closed more than 240 accounts. Bakyt Sydykov, the Special Representative of the President of the Kyrgyz Republic for Special Assignments on Sanctions Policy and the Mitigation of Sanctions Risks, announced the figures. According to him, the Kyrgyz Republic is giving particularly careful consideration to the concerns expressed by the European Union, the United Kingdom and the United States regarding the risk that third countries may be used to circumvent sanctions, including in the context of the activities of the A7 network and the A7A5 stablecoin. Related news Kyrgyzstan to shut down more than 100 companies to mitigate sanctions risks "Our position is unequivocal: the territory, jurisdiction, and banking and payment infrastructure of the Kyrgyz Republic must not be used for transactions intended to circumvent sanctions. Government agencies, regulators and financial institutions are taking steps to detect and put a stop to any attempt at such activity, and to guard against the risk of it being conducted through affiliated entities, intermediaries or new payment channels,” Bakyt Sydykov said. This work serves the national interests of Kyrgyzstan. Its purpose is to safeguard the resilience of the financial system, to foster the conditions for legitimate trade, and to preserve access for citizens and businesses to international payments, investment and capital markets, he added. The mitigation of sanctions risks remains under the personal oversight of the President of the Kyrgyz Republic, Sadyr Japarov. Government agencies have been tasked with ensuring a coordinated approach to identifying risks, taking the measures provided for by law and monitoring their implementation. The Kyrgyz Republic pursues an independent foreign and economic policy and develops mutually beneficial relations with its international partners. Differences in political and legal assessments of particular restrictive measures do not stand in the way of practical cooperation in preventing sanctions circumvention and protecting the financial system. Government agencies are reviewing companies, analyzing cross-border payments, and establishing the ultimate beneficial owners and the economic purpose of higher-risk transactions. According to the competent authorities, as at October 26, 2026, 52 legal entities have ceased operations as part of the work to mitigate sanctions risks, and compulsory liquidation proceedings are under way in respect of a further 57. State-owned banks have closed more than 240 accounts. Reviews of other companies are ongoing. These figures reflect the work as a whole and do not relate exclusively to A7 and A7A5. Related news Sanctions: Kyrgyzstan announces liquidation of state-backed USDKG stablecoin Preventive measures have been taken in respect of market participants linked to A7 and A7A5. The financial market regulator (Finnadzor) has revoked the licenses of a number of market participants. The Cabinet of Ministers has also taken decisions to liquidate a number of organizations. Materials concerning other entities have been referred to the competent authorities for review. Government agencies have been instructed to ensure that the decisions taken are implemented and that the restrictions provided for by law are observed. This work includes identifying affiliated entities and the payment channels they use, as well as the persons exercising de facto control over them. It is essential to prevent any attempt to carry on similar activity under new names, through newly registered companies or by shifting operations to other intermediaries. All measures are taken on lawful grounds, with due regard to the orderly completion of transactions and the protection of customers' legitimate rights. The fact that a review is being conducted does not in itself indicate any wrongdoing. In the banking sector, the National Bank, together with commercial banks, is strengthening procedures for customer identification, the identification of ultimate beneficial owners and the verification of the purpose of payments. Particular attention is paid to transactions whose economic rationale is inconsistent with a customer's stated business, as well as to settlements involving intermediaries and related parties. Banks report to the National Bank on a monthly basis on closed accounts, blocked payments and refusals of service. The regulator, in turn, provides banks with information on elevated risks, together with guidance and recommendations. International consultants have been engaged to carry out an independent assessment of the existing systems. The priority is to identify risk before a transaction takes place. Checks should cover the client's ownership structure, its ultimate beneficiaries and the circumstances of the payment. At the same time, controls must be proportionate to the risk and must not deprive law-abiding citizens and businesses of the ability to make legitimate payments. Further measures are being prepared in the field of virtual assets. The National Agency for Virtual Assets and Blockchain Technologies is drafting a Decree of the President of the Kyrgyz Republic providing for enhanced sanctions screening, the establishment of liability for market participants, and mechanisms for restricting transactions where there are lawful grounds to do so. The draft Decree provides for screening against the sanctions lists of the United Nations, the European Union, the United Kingdom and the United States. The legal basis and procedure for applying restrictive measures are determined by the legislation of the Kyrgyz Republic and its international obligations. In parallel, a Unified Digital Platform for the Licensing and Supervision of Virtual Asset Service Providers is being established. It is intended to provide automated screening of applicants, transaction monitoring and analysis of crypto wallets. Further work will involve expanding the use of blockchain analytics and strengthening risk-based supervision of market participants. Responsible engagement by the business community remains an essential part of preventing sanctions risks. We call on entrepreneurs to carry out due diligence on their counterparties and their ultimate beneficial owners, to assess the economic substance of transactions, and to take applicable restrictions into account. Particular caution is warranted in respect of any proposal to conceal the true party to a payment, to state a false purpose of payment, or to use an intermediary whose economic role is unclear. Government agencies will continue to explain the applicable requirements and to keep businesses informed of identified risks. At the same time, the State will, within its competence, assist in protecting the legitimate rights of citizens and organizations of the Kyrgyz Republic, including where they are designated under sanctions regimes. Such protection entails establishing the facts of each case, providing verifiable information and making use of the procedures available in the relevant jurisdiction. "The Kyrgyz Republic stands ready to engage in regular professional dialogue with the competent authorities of the European Union, its Member States the United Kingdom and the United States. We will give due consideration to well-documented information on risks and will share information on the measures taken through established channels, in accordance with the law and confidentiality requirements,” Sydikov noted. "The Kyrgyz Republic publicly reaffirms its determination to identify and put a stop to any transactions aimed at circumventing sanctions through its jurisdiction and financial infrastructure. We will continue to monitor the implementation of the decisions taken and to prevent any attempt at similar activity through related person

https://en.kabar.kg/news/fuel-arrives-in.body: Bishkek, Oct. 28, 2026. /Kabar/. Today, October 28, the first shipments of fuel from China began arriving in Kyrgyzstan via railway. Kanatbek Eshatov, President of the Association of Oil Traders told Kabar during meeting dedicated to ensuring Kyrgyzstan's energy stability. According to him, while fuel was previously imported into Kyrgyzstan primarily from Russia, it is now also being supplied from countries such as Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Belarus, and Turkiye. "In August, during the summer our representatives, accompanied by government officials, visited China and signed agreements with major Chinese companies there. Initially, fuel was being transported by road. However, today, October 28, the first shipments from China have begun entering Kyrgyzstan by rail," he stated. According to Eshatov, the situation regarding diesel fuel in Kyrgyzstan is currently stable. However, there is a slight shortage of gasoline, making it impossible to purchase the desired quantities. Consequently, the country is seeking various fuel-supplying nations and working to increase supply volumes. "The situation with diesel fuel in Kyrgyzstan is currently stable. We are experiencing a slight shortage of gasoline; we are unable to purchase the volumes we would like. We aim to increase our domestic reserves, ideally, we would like to build up a 2 to 3-month supply of gasoline," said the president of the association. According to his data, daily consumption in Kyrgyzstan amounts to 1,200 tons of gasoline and an equivalent volume of diesel fuel. Total daily domestic consumption is approximately 2,500 to 3,000 tons. Furthermore, repair and renovation work is underway at Kyrgyzstan's two major fuel refineries, the facilities located in Jalal-Abad and Kara-Balta. Modernization efforts, including the installation of state-of-the-art equipment, are currently in progress at these plants. "Repair and maintenance work is currently underway at two refineries. Modernization is taking place, and new, state-of-the-art equipment is being installed. Once they become operational next year, the situation regarding fuel in Kyrgyzstan should change. That is what we are aiming for," noted Kanatbek Eshatov. Print

Yesterday, 22:00 1 min read 2 650 views 0 comments 0 Source: Unsplash Uzbekistan remained the largest source of foreign workers entering Russia in the first half of 2026, with 1.18mn Uzbek citizens arriving to work, according to Russia’s state news agency TASS. The figure stood at 1,178,609, ahead of Tajikistan, whose citizens accounted for 494,518 arrivals, and Kyrgyzstan, with 289,061. Kazakhstan ranked fourth with 122,654, followed by China with 89,656. The top 10 also included Armenia with 88,629 arrivals, Azerbaijan with 62,440, India with 27,419, Turkmenistan with 13,428 and Türkiye with 8,360. Russia applies different employment requirements to foreign nationals depending on their country of citizenship. Citizens of Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Azerbaijan can work in Russia using a labor patent, while nationals of Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Armenia are exempt from this requirement. Citizens of China, India, Turkmenistan and Türkiye must obtain work visas and work permits. https://www.azernews.az/region/266377.ht.body: We do not see our return to CSTO says Armenia's Mirzoyan 28 October 2026 15:45 (UTC+04:00) Akbar Novruz Read more Armenia has ruled out resuming its participation in the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), reaffirming that its membership remains frozen and that Yerevan has no intention of reversing its position. Armenian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Trade Ararat Mirzoyan made the remarks during a press conference on Wednesday, responding to statements by former CSTO Secretary General Nikolay Bordyuzha, who had called for Armenia's expulsion from the Russia-led security alliance. "We [i.e. Armenia] have long since stopped our participation in the CSTO's work, and we have frozen our membership. If other members or the secretary-general of that structure are making any comments, [it is] in vain. We will not change our attitude and, also, we do not see our return to the CSTO," Mirzoyan stated. His remarks followed Bordyuzha's earlier assertion that Armenia should be expelled from the organisation. Mirzoyan's response indicates that Yerevan considers discussions over its continued membership largely irrelevant to its current foreign policy position, given that the country has already suspended its participation in the alliance's activities. Although Armenia has frozen its membership, it has not formally withdrawn from the CSTO. The distinction means that the country remains a member of the organisation while declining to participate in its work. The latest exchange underscores the continuing tensions between Armenia and the Russia-led security bloc, with Yerevan maintaining that it sees no prospect of returning to active participation. Mirzoyan's statement also signals that calls from former or current CSTO officials are unlikely to influence Armenia's position on its future within the alliance. https://english.news.cn/20261028/f720074.body: Interview: China's economy shows resilience, vitality, says Kyrgyz economist-Xinhua Interview: China's economy shows resilience, vitality, says Kyrgyz economist Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-10-28 14:02:30 BISHKEK, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's economy is demonstrating resilience and vitality through positive development trends despite various challenges, Kyrgyz economist Iskender Sharsheev told Xinhua. In the first three quarters of 2026, China's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.6 percent year on year, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics. In the third quarter, China's GDP expanded 4.5 percent year on year, up from 4.3 percent in the previous quarter. "Stable economic growth points to the country's new achievements in high-quality development," Sharsheev said, adding that the growth is driven by favorable trends in high-tech manufacturing, services and exports. He also highlighted the strong performance of China's foreign trade in the first three quarters of 2026. The country's total imports and exports rose by 18.8 percent year on year, according the National Bureau of Statistics. During the same period, trade with countries participating in the China-proposed Belt and Road Initiative surged 17.1 percent. "These results in China's foreign trade are driven by strong demand for its products from advanced sectors, including integrated circuits, electric vehicles and lithium batteries, as well as by market diversification, resilient industrial and supply chains, and the determined implementation of a policy of high-quality opening-up," the economist said. For Kyrgyzstan, a country along the Belt and Road, China's expanding foreign trade presents significant opportunities to increase exports of agricultural products and mineral resources, as well as transit services, Sharsheev said. It also helps attract Chinese investment in infrastructure, logistics and processing industries, while strengthening Kyrgyzstan's role as a regional transport hub, he added. Effectively leveraging these opportunities could help Kyrgyzstan create jobs, boost foreign exchange earnings and speed up its economic modernization, he said. "Foreign trade continues to provide strong support for the industrial sector. The Chinese government has expressed confidence in achieving these goals and retains considerable policy space to introduce targeted stimulus measures. Together, these factors provide a solid foundation for China to meet its year-end economic targets," Sharsheev added. ■ Interview: China's economy shows resilience, vitality, says Kyrgyz economist

https://kaktus.media/doc/555824_smi:_bol.body: kaktus.media СМИ: Болсонару уехал с семьей в США после поражения на президентских выборах в Бразилии В мире 1065 28 октября 2026 08:31 Kaktus Все самое интересное в Telegram Бразильский сенатор Флавио Болсонару покинул страну и направился в США после поражения на президентских выборах, состоявшихся в воскресенье. Об этом во вторник сообщили Reuters три источника. В Госдепартаменте США заявили, что сенатору и членам его семьи будут выданы въездные визы. Читайте также: В Бразилии выбрали президента Болсонару, который пока официально не признал поражение от действующего президента Бразилии Луиса Инасиу Лулы да Силвы, уехал из страны, несмотря на решение Верховного суда, предписавшего ему сдать паспорта. Судебное постановление связано с расследованием дела об отмывании денег. Политик отрицает свою причастность к противоправным действиям. Флавио Болсонару выступает после проигрыша на выборах. Фото Reuters / Adriano Machado. Местонахождение самого Болсонару, его супруги и двух дочерей первоначально оставалось неизвестным. Один из источников, близких к семье, сообщил, что сенатор прибыл во Флориду, однако не уточнил, в какой именно город. "Госдепартамент выдаст визы Флавио Болсонару и членам его семьи и разрешит им въезд в Соединенные Штаты", - заявил высокопоставленный представитель американского внешнеполитического ведомства. Отъезд Болсонару может обострить отношения Бразилии и США Отъезд сенатора грозит углубить разногласия между двумя крупнейшими по численности населения странами Америки. Лула да Силва обвинял Вашингтон в сотрудничестве с семьей Болсонару с целью вернуть ее представителей к власти. Ранее Reuters сообщало о кампании внутри администрации США, направленной на восстановление политических позиций клана Болсонару. Президент США Дональд Трамп ранее утверждал, что отец Флавио, бывший президент Бразилии Жаир Болсонару, стал жертвой судебного преследования. После поражения на выборах 2022 года Жаир Болсонару также уехал в США, когда американским президентом был Джо Байден. Позднее он вернулся в Бразилию, где впоследствии был приговорен к 27 годам лишения свободы за участие в заговоре с целью государственного переворота после штурма его сторонниками правительственных зданий в Бразилиа. В понедельник Трамп не прокомментировал отъезд Флавио Болсонару, однако заявил журналистам, что бразильские выборы "похожи на очередные сфальсифицированные выборы". Лула да Силва, выступая в Бразилиа, сообщил, что только что узнал об отъезде сенатора. Президент назвал случившееся постыдным и заявил, что Болсонару следовало остаться в стране и доказывать свою невиновность. Флавио Болсонару считался фаворитом воскресных выборов, однако в итоге потерпел неожиданное поражение от Лулы да Силвы. Верховный суд потребовал сдать паспорта В понедельник Болсонару было предписано в течение 24 часов передать паспорта властям. После истечения установленного срока документы были аннулированы, сообщили два источника Reuters. В постановлении Верховного суда, с которым ознакомилось агентство, отмечалось, что существует риск бегства политика из Бразилии. Суд также указал на наличие у него "значительных финансовых ресурсов" в качестве одного из оснований для изъятия паспортов. В феврале после окончания срока полномочий в Сенате Болсонару лишится депутатского иммунитета от уголовного преследования. В понедельник он утверждал, что не собирается покидать страну. "Я никогда не думал об отъезде из страны. Я сдам паспорта и буду защищаться от этого фарса, который является очевидной попыткой запугать меня", - заявил сенатор. Новость об отъезде, судя по всему, стала неожиданностью даже для его предвыборного штаба. "Мы удивлены этой новостью, поскольку еще вчера обсуждали необходимость того, чтобы Флавио - учитывая 60 миллионов полученных им голосов - взял на себя роль лидера оппозиции", - заявил журналистам сенатор Рожериу Маринью, руководитель кампании Болсонару. Флавио Болсонару пока официально не признал поражение. В воскресенье он заявил, что намерен добиваться аннулирования результатов выборов, ссылаясь на предполагаемые нарушения при голосовании. Однако уже в понедельник его Либеральная партия признала победу Лулы да Силвы. Обстоятельства выезда сенатора из страны остаются неясными: неизвестно, как он смог покинуть Бразилию, несмотря на судебное предписание о сдаче паспортов в течение суток. Высокопоставленный представитель Федеральной полиции заявил, что Болсонару не пересекал границу через обычный пункт миграционного контроля. Младший брат сенатора Эдуардо Болсонару, проживающий в США, еще до голосования говорил, что поражение на выборах должно стать поводом для отъезда Флавио. "Если мой брат не победит, я считаю, что ему следует покинуть страну", - заявил он в этом месяце в разговоре с подкастером Стивеном Краудером. выборы США Бразилия Есть новость или проблема? https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/society/.body: Home Azerbaijan Society Azerbaijan has over 300 youth NGOs, deputy minister says Society News 27 October 2026 18:49 (UTC +04:00) Photo: Trend News Agency Firaya Nurizada Correspondent Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. More than 300 youth nongovernmental organizations are operating in Azerbaijan, the Deputy Minister of Youth and Sports, Farhad Hajiyev, said during the discussion “Intercultural Leadership for a Shared Future,” held on Tuesday as part of the World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue, Trend 's correspondent reports from the event. The deputy minister noted that the country has approximately 2 million schoolchildren and 200,000 university students. According to him, they represent Azerbaijan’s future leadership potential and human capital. Hajiyev noted that, although the modern world has become more interconnected, the expansion of these ties does not always lead to greater mutual understanding. “Despite the opportunities offered by globalization and technology, we are witnessing a rise in polarization, mistrust, and disunity within societies. Under such conditions, intercultural leadership ceases to be merely a desirable quality and becomes a vital responsibility,” he emphasized. According to the deputy minister, true leadership does not lie in bringing everyone to a single position, but in uniting diverse perspectives around a common goal. An effective leader must be able to listen to others before making decisions, respect differences without compromising their principles, and build trust even in the face of disagreement. Hajiyev said that intercultural dialogue has long been an important national value and a strategic priority for Azerbaijan. The Baku Process, initiated by President Ilham Aliyev in 2008, is a testament to the country’s commitment to promoting mutual understanding, cultural diversity, and cooperation among civilizations. He noted that investing in the leadership potential of young people is one of the most important investments a country can make in its future. At the same time, leadership cannot be developed solely based on theoretical knowledge. It requires experience, responsibility, mentorship, and opportunities to collaborate with people who think differently. The Deputy Minister welcomed UNESCO’s “Youth for Peace” program on intercultural leadership. According to him, the program brings together 50 young leaders selected from more than 8,000 applications from around the world. “Developing leadership qualities is not only about preparing people for high-level positions, but also about preparing them to bring about positive change,” Hajiyev added. https://cabar.asia/en/why-are-new-approa.body: © CABAR - Central Asian Bureau for Analytical Reporting Please make active links to the source, when using materials from this website На русском Approaches to the promotion of human rights in the field of freedom of religion in Kazakhstan by international legal institutions require in-depth study and a more flexible approach. Successfully building of a new format of dialogue is possible only if the existing realities are taken into account. Illustrative photo. Photo from news.un.org For example, in its 2024 report , the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom again recommended that the U.S. Department of State place Kazakhstan on the Special Watch List for ‘tolerance of serious violations of religious freedom’ along with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Turkey and other countries. International organizations have for many years criticized the existing 2011 law ‘On Religious Activity and Religious Associations’. In particular, the fact that it requires mandatory registration of religious associations, religious expertise and ‘accreditation’ of missionary activities. All of this, according to international and local human rights activists, violates international legal norms concerning freedom of religion or belief, which Kazakhstan once ratified. In response, state authorities claim that international norms do not take into account the specific local context of the country and the complex geopolitical situation in the region. Thus, in a report prepared by the Institute for War and Peace Reporting (IWPR) in 2023, a representative of the Committee on Religious Affairs of the Ministry of Culture and Information of Kazakhstan said that religious expertise, for example, is necessary to ensure public safety and counter threats of religious extremism and terrorism. It is not difficult to notice that in their responses to international criticism, state bodies appeal to the experience of other countries and never directly criticize the international norms themselves. Kazakhstan often participates in dialogue platforms organized by the UN, the OSCE or the US government. All of this emphasizes how important a positive international image is for a state. Nevertheless, 13 years have passed since the law was adopted in 2011 and, despite all the criticism, no significant changes have been made to the law. As practice shows, in the balance between national security and international standards of freedom of religion or belief, the state prefers to lean more towards the former. Most likely, according to the authorities, limiting religious freedom is a necessary sacrifice to ensure stability within the country. Many officials see ‘excessive’ freedom of religion as a threat in the form of uncontrolled spread of violent extremist ideas. Ineffectiveness of existing approaches International human rights institutions in their attempts to promote freedom of religion or belief in Central Asia, and in particular in Kazakhstan, use the so-called ‘name and shame’ method, publicly criticizing states for anti-democratic laws. In this way, international actors try to hold state systems accountable for human rights violations and highlight the problems in the international arena. However, as research in the field of international relations shows, such a strategy most often leads to a response in the form of the status quo protection, thus increasing tensions between the parties – the international community and individual countries. This applies to the case of Kazakhstan as well. Since 2005, international criticism has not helped to seriously change the state’s policy towards religion and each subsequent change in the law has been harsher and harsher. Kazakhstan keeps stating that such measures are necessary to protect society in the context of the complex situation in the region and the world. Certainly, attracting international attention and subsequent criticism is one of the important tools for ensuring human rights. Local human rights defenders and civil society, having no other alternatives to influence the government domestically, turn to international agencies. In turn, the international community, be it the UN, the OSCE, or the US State Department, prepare reports that reflect current problems. Such an approach seems logical, consistent and optimal for the promotion of human rights. However, without detracting from the effectiveness of this approach, it is worth understanding all the nuances and complexity of its consequences in practice. For example, the creation of ‘blacklists’ such as the ‘special watch list’, although initially intended to attract international attention at the political level, more often than not does not change the situation. This is confirmed not only in the case of Kazakhstan, but also by scientific evidence . Analyzing the situation in 145 countries from 1975 to 2000, researcher Hafner-Burton concludes that in many cases governments, under pressure from international criticism, make rather cosmetic changes, but in fact continue or even worsen the situation of human rights violations. Public denigration, so often practiced by a wide variety of human rights organizations, has the effect of placing the criticized states outside the community of ‘civilized countries,’ thereby creating an even greater gap in dialogue, which leads to even greater isolation of these countries. What to do? Given these dynamics, it seems more effective to create strategies of interaction based on a positive approach. Firstly, international actors need to pay more attention to understanding the root causes of the existing paradigm within Kazakhstan. Only by understanding the motives behind the actions of the authorities can we gradually move towards a dialogue based on trust and cooperation. Second, international organizations need to move away from a public censure approach. Instead, more attention should be paid to the policy of encouraging positive actions of the authorities, even if they seem insignificant and insufficient. The development of positive indicators will motivate public authorities to make more changes and strengthen relationships with the international community. Third, there is a need for training for public officials of all ranks on international standards in the field of religion. It is very important that these trainings not be top-down or instructive in tone. The training should demonstrate how freedom of religion or belief can improve national security, not undermine it. Formal appeals for compliance with international norms will not suffice. Practical examples are needed. Thus, the effectiveness of an international approach to advancing human rights in the area of religion requires a profound change in the very foundations of engagement. Successfully building a new format of dialogue also requires international actors to be flexible, innovative, and willing to reevaluate strategies that have been approved over the years. This, in turn, will lead to the formation of a new paradigm, despite growing fragmentation and globalization fatigue. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/28/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan widens Presidential Olympiad to 35 sports Uzbekistan will expand its Presidential Olympiad to 35 sports and open the competition to athletes aged 14 to 17, while introducing one-year scholarships for winners from 2027 and continuing to send 50 top performers to international training camps each year. Today, 13:00 1 min read 1 055 views 0 comments 0 Source: Presidential Press Service Uzbekistan will expand the Presidential Olympiad program to 35 sports and extend eligibility to athletes aged 14 to 17, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced at an event at the Olympic Village. The competition’s age category has been expanded, while 50 winners will continue to be sent to international training camps abroad each year. Starting in 2027, winners will also receive one-year scholarships. The sports school achieving the best results in its respective discipline will be provided with the necessary equipment, according to the announcement. The Museum of Olympic Glory in Tashkent will also be relocated to the Olympic Village, giving young athletes an opportunity to learn about the history and achievements of Uzbekistan’s champions. Mirziyoyev called on young people to make use of the opportunities available to them through discipline, knowledge and persistent effort. He then declared the 2026 Presidential Olympiad open. “ "Believe in yourself! Work on yourself! Be worthy of your Motherland! https://kz.kursiv.media/en/2026-10-28/en.body: President Tokayev proposes higher taxes for the wealthy in Kazakhstan Published October 28, 2026 16:08 Tanat Kozhmanov Senior Editor t.kozhmanov@kursiv.media Zhanbolat Mamyshev Senior Journalist of the Business News department zh.mamyshev@kursiv.media kazakhstan president tokayev taxation The president believes the time has come to discuss introducing higher taxes on the wealthy / Collage by Kursiv.media, photo editor: Adelina Mamedova President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev believes Kazakhstan should discuss a higher tax rate for individuals with large fortunes. «I’d like to specifically address the issue of tax fairness. I believe it is time to discuss introducing a higher rate for those who possess large fortunes,» he said in his address to the nation. The president emphasized that the government has no intention of restricting legally acquired assets. «Doing so would contradict the Constitution. This is about a fair contribution from every citizen toward the development of our country. It is a matter of fairness,» he said. Tokayev noted that the government and the Kurultai have been tasked with examining the issue and putting forward proposals. He also argued that tax fairness requires transparency, which in turn requires full digitalization. In this regard, he proposed using advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, more actively within the tax system. Kazakhstan has discussed introducing a «luxury tax» on several previous occasions. Currently, the country has no separate luxury tax. However, starting in 2026, higher taxes and excise duties apply to certain high-value assets. Real estate valued at over $983,858 is subject to a 2% tax rate. A 10% excise duty also applies to automobiles valued at 18,000 MCI (monthly calculation index) or more, as well as yachts and aircraft valued at 24,000 MCI or more. Additionally, a progressive personal income tax (PIT) scale took effect in 2026, under which a 15% rate applies only to the portion of annual taxable income exceeding 8,500 MCI ($80,375 in 2026). https://vlast.kz/english/71391-kazakhsta.body: Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev delivered his annual Address to the Nation on October 28, repeating his call for the country to become a “ large-scale construction site ,” while announcing broader plans to boost economic growth in a 95-minute speech before Parliament. In his address — traditionally delivered in September — Tokayev outlined the government’s priorities for the current parliamentary session, including expanding transport links, increasing power generation capacity, and drawing on the National Fund to finance infrastructure and social projects under a new initiative dubbed “Halyqtyq Qurylys” (“People’s Construction”). “The government needs to develop an unprecedented infrastructure modernization plan. By the end of 2029, the National Fund will allocate approximately 6.5 trillion tenge ($14.3 billion) for this large-scale project. Over the remainder of this year and in the first two months of 2027, 1.5 trillion tenge ($3.3 billion) will be allocated to launch social investment projects,” Tokayev said. Declaring 2027 the “Year of Nationwide Large-Scale Construction,” Tokayev noted that the “country’s national response” to the “coming era of artificial intelligence” would be to “build, build, build,” particularly through the development of new transport infrastructure, housing, research centers, and healthcare facilities. Tokayev suggested that these ambitions would also require addressing the country’s persistent electricity shortages, reiterating the government's goal of achieving a sustained electricity surplus by 2029. Denouncing a “botched” thermal power plant in Balkhash and delays to other projects, Tokaeyev said that reaching energy self-sufficiency would require modernizing existing facilities and transmission lines, expanding what he described as “clean” coal-fired generation, and building new power plants. To this end, Tokayev restated his intentions to create a state strategic uranium reserve to support the country’s two proposed nuclear power plants near Lake Balkash, whose construction he suggested should be expedited over the coming years. “I believe it is possible — and perhaps even necessary — to begin construction of the Balkhash NPP as early as next year and to sign a comprehensive cooperation agreement to start the construction of the Moyinkum NPP as soon as possible,” Tokayev said. During his comments, Tokayev introduced several new initiatives to make conditions for doing business in Kazakhstan more favorable. He first criticized poor coordination among government bodies responsible for attracting foreign investment, calling for the state-owned Baiterek holding company to play a greater role in coordinating investment efforts. Tokayev also argued that attracting foreign investment would also require a “high-quality” justice system, proposing the establishment of specialized independent common-law courts in Alatau, a technology city under development in Almaty region. Finally, noting that the share of small and medium-sized enterprises in Kazakhstan's GDP had reached 40%, Tokayev asked the parliament and government to discuss the extension of a three-year moratorium on financial, environmental, and labor inspections of these businesses. Towards the end of his remarks, Tokayev instructed the government to increase the minimum wage from 85,000 ($185) to 110,000 tenge ($240), effective January 1, a move that he says would increase the incomes of 1.8 million people. Moments later, Tokayev called for an overhaul to the country’s social benefits system , echoing criticisms he made of welfare spending in last year’s address . “Such so-called ‘kindness’ toward the people at the expense of the budget is nothing but populism, cynically masking all manner of schemes directed against the interests of the people and the country’s sustainable development,” the president said. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/10/28/zari.body: Share asia+ Categories Governance Politics Tajikistan Format News Published 28.10.2026 15:49 Translations Eng Рус Тоҷ Tajikistan’s lower house of parliament has approved Zarif Alizoda’s appointment as chairman of the Central Commission for Elections and Referendums (CCER), replacing Bakhtiyor Khudoyorzoda, who had led the commission for two decades. Lawmakers also approved a new deputy chairman and five commission members. The decision was made at a session of the Majlisi Namoyandagon on October 28, following President Emomali Rahmon’s nomination of Alizoda on October 26, the parliament’s press service reported. Under Article 57 of Tajikistan’s Constitution, the Majlisi Namoyandagon is authorized to form the Central Commission for Elections and Referendums and elect or recall its chairperson, deputy chairperson and members upon the president’s recommendation. Alongside approving Alizoda’s appointment, lawmakers voted to relieve Khudoyorzoda of his duties as commission chairman. They also approved the recall of deputy chairman Abdujabbor Qodirzoda and commission members Nosirjon Salimi, Makhfirat Khidirzoda, Yusufbek Shodmonbek, Navrouz Samadzoda and Muiston Azizi. Jamshed Saidzoda was approved as the new deputy chairman. The newly approved commission members are Dilafrouz Nazaralizoda, Adham Mamourzoda, Zaynura Rajabzoda, Navrouz Samadzoda and Makhfirat Khidirzoda. The changes were attributed to the expiration of the previous members’ terms of office. Anvar Safarzoda, the president’s newly appointed aide for legal affairs and authorized representative in both chambers of parliament, addressed lawmakers during the session. He took over the legal affairs post from Alizoda and had previously served as the president’s aide for social development and public relations for nine months. Who is Zarif Alizoda? Alizoda is a lawyer who has held several senior government positions. From 2009 to 2019, he served two terms as Tajikistan’s first human rights ombudsman. From 2006 to 2009, he was the president’s state adviser on legal policy and authorized representative in both chambers of parliament. He also served on the Commission on National Reconciliation from 1997 to 2000 and was a member of the Majlisi Namoyandagon from 2000 to 2001. Presidential election expected in 2027 Tajikistan’s next presidential election is expected to take place in 2027. The previous presidential election was held in 2020, while parliamentary elections took place in 2025. The October 28 parliamentary session also considered additional financing agreements with the International Development Association for the Early Childhood Development Project for Human Capital Enhancement in Tajikistan and the Agriculture Resilience Enhancement Project. Lawmakers also adopted draft laws proposing amendments to legislation on state administration bodies, geodesy and cartography, education, public-private partnerships and personal subsidiary farming. https://www.azernews.az/nation/266307.ht.body: Azerbaijan Prosecutor General meets Anti-Corruption officials from Maldives and Egypt 27 October 2026 15:48 (UTC+04:00) Qabil Ashirov Read more Azerbaijan Prosecutor General Kamran Aliyev has held separate meetings with Adam Shamil, chairman of the Anti-Corruption Commission of the Maldives, and Amr Adel Hosni, head of Egypt's Administrative Control Authority, to discuss cooperation in combating corruption. According to the Prosecutor General's Office, the meetings took place ahead of the third high-level meeting of heads of law enforcement agencies responsible for combating corruption in member states of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), scheduled to be held in Baku on October 27–28. During the meetings, Aliyev outlined the legal and institutional reforms implemented in Azerbaijan under the leadership of President Ilham Aliyev. He highlighted efforts to improve transparency and accountability in public administration, strengthen anti-corruption mechanisms and prevent corruption risks. During his meeting with Hosni, the sides emphasised that relations between Azerbaijan and Egypt were based on longstanding friendship and mutual respect. They highlighted the importance of high-level political dialogue between the two countries, referring to President Ilham Aliyev's meeting with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi during his official visit to Egypt on June 8, 2024. The officials also underscored the importance of cooperation within the United Nations, the Non-Aligned Movement and the OIC. The discussions focused on expanding ties between Azerbaijan's Prosecutor General's Office, including its Anti-Corruption General Directorate, and Egypt's Administrative Control Authority. The sides explored opportunities to exchange experience in preventing, detecting and investigating corruption offences and implementing effective oversight mechanisms. During his meeting with Shamil, the sides noted that diplomatic relations between Azerbaijan and the Maldives were established in 1994. They emphasised the importance of developing political dialogue and strengthening cooperation within international organisations. The meeting also recalled Maldivian President Mohamed Muizzu's visit to Azerbaijan and participation in the COP29 climate conference. The officials discussed measures to prevent and detect corruption offences, expand information exchange, share best practices and improve the effectiveness of international legal cooperation. Aliyev also recalled the participation of a member of the Maldivian Anti-Corruption Commission in the sixth plenary meeting of the Global Operational Network of Anti-Corruption Law Enforcement Authorities (GlobE Network) and the network's 10th Steering Committee meeting, held in Baku in May 2025. He highlighted the importance of these platforms in strengthening international anti-corruption cooperation. Both meetings emphasised the need to deepen institutional cooperation, exchange best practices and expand coordination through international platforms. The parties expressed mutual interest in further developing ties between their respective institutions. Tags: Azerbaijan OIC Egypt corruption anti-corruption

https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/4239864..body: Home Azerbaijan Azerbaijan's education must align with labor market needs – deputy minister Azerbaijan News 27 October 2026 18:07 (UTC +04:00) Sadig Javadov Economic Journalist Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. Azerbaijan’s education system must be aligned with the changing needs of the labor market and economy, Deputy Minister of Science and Education Hasan Hasanli said at the opening ceremony of the IE Leadership and Innovation Center in Baku on Tuesday, Trend 's correspondent reports from the event. According to him, efforts to train specialists with modern skills and expand cooperation with the private sector remain key priorities. He said the rapid growth in the volume of information in the age of artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new challenges for the education system. Under these conditions, education needs both traditional approaches that support long-term development and flexible models that respond quickly to the changing needs of the economy and industry. “There is a difference between an approach that involves waiting 10–15 years to produce better graduates and the fast, flexible approach required by industry, companies and the economy. Under current conditions, it is important to reconcile these two approaches,” the deputy minister said. Hasanli noted that Azerbaijan has been implementing a series of measures since 2013 under the education development strategy approved by President Ilham Aliyev. According to him, the program has helped improve the quality and accessibility of education. The deputy minister also referred to the results of international assessments, noting that Azerbaijan has made progress in education in recent years, particularly in subjects such as mathematics, which are important for various industries. He said the country’s performance in this area had approached the average levels of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). He stressed that sustained government efforts are helping develop a pool of talented young people whose potential can be further nurtured. To realize this potential, it is important to systematically develop their knowledge and skills and prepare them to become future leaders, managers and professionals. Hasanli also highlighted changes in the higher education system. He said initiatives such as the Baku Higher Oil School, the French-Azerbaijani University (UFAZ), the Azerbaijan-Türkiye University and dual-degree programs play an important role in training highly qualified professionals. According to the deputy minister, aligning education with labor market needs is impossible without close cooperation with the private sector. In this regard, partnerships with PASHA Holding, SOCAR, and other companies are particularly important. “One of the main challenges is addressing the mismatch between labor market needs and the education system. Cooperation with the private sector makes it possible to identify these needs more accurately and acquire the relevant knowledge. The AI Hub platform was also established to ensure the continuity of this cooperation,” he said. Hasanli added that a meeting of the steering committee had discussed initial projects being implemented jointly with IE University and the Ministry of Economy, the work of the observatory and other initiatives. He said the main goal of the cooperation was to connect the potential developed through education with the real needs of the economy, accelerate the training of specialists equipped with modern technologies and expand the country’s innovation capacity.
